A systematic review was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science until January 2026 to search for studies including patients with a diagnosis of intracapsular TMD as participants; physical therapy or physical therapy combined to other conservative approaches as intervention; placebo, sham treatments, oral pharmacological anti-inflammatory drugs, behavioral therapy, or other conservative approaches as comparison; maximal mouth opening (MMO) as outcome. Out of 1578 identified records, 10 studies were included. A total of 354 subjects were analyzed, of which 213 performed a rehabilitation technique and 141 were included in the control group. Although the randomized trials reported improvement in MMO, pain, and function, a major limitation was the lack of standardized physiotherapy protocols across trials. Findings from the present systematic review showed that physiotherapy (active and passive jaw exercises, associated with relaxation techniques) might improve MMO. Further studies with uniform protocols and high-quality randomized trials are needed to validate the efficacy of multimodal treatments in arthrogenic TMD subtypes.

titre: Photobiomodulation therapy has a negligible effect as an adjunct to motor control exercise in people with chronic non-specific low back pain: a randomised trial.
auteurs: Tomazoni Shaiane Silva, de Oliveira Marcelo Ferreira Duarte, Schardong Jociane, Plentz Rodrigo Della Méa, Casalechi Heliodora Leão, Teixeira Ighor Luiz Azevedo, Serra Andrey Jorge, Leal-Junior Ernesto Cesar Pinto, Bjordal Jan Magnus
resume: In adults with chronic non-specific low back pain, does adding photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) to a program of motor control exercise (MCE) improve pain intensity, disability and circulating prostaglandin E<sub>2</sub> (PGE<sub>2</sub>) concentrations compared with sham PBMT plus MCE? A randomised controlled trial was conducted with concealed allocation, intention-to-treat analysis and blinding of participants, therapists and assessors. Adults aged 18 to 65 years seeking treatment for chronic non-specific low back pain of ≥ 3 months in duration. Participants were randomly allocated to active PBMT plus MCE or sham PBMT plus MCE. Both groups received 12 treatment sessions over 6 weeks. Assessments were completed at baseline and 6 weeks, with follow-up assessments at 1 month after the end of the intervention period and at 3, 6 and 12 months after randomisation. Primary outcomes were pain intensity (0 to 10 numerical rating scale) and disability (0 to 24 Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire) at 6 weeks, in which higher scores indicated greater severity. Secondary outcomes were: pain and disability at follow-up timepoints; circulating PGE<sub>2</sub> concentrations at 6 weeks; and medication use, concomitant care and adverse events throughout the follow-up period. A total of 148 participants were randomised (74 per group). The intention-to-treat analysis showed that PBMT plus MCE had a negligible effect compared with sham plus MCE at 6 weeks for pain intensity (MD -0.4 points, 95% CI -1.2 to 0.4), disability (MD -0.7 points, 95% CI -2.4 to 0.9) or circulating PGE<sub>2</sub> concentrations (MD 31 pg/ml, 95% CI -4 to 66). Negligible between-group differences were observed throughout the 12-month follow-up period, and no treatment-related adverse events occurred. Adding PBMT to MCE did not provide clinically important additional improvements in pain intensity, disability or circulating PGE<sub>2</sub> concentrations compared with sham plus the same exercise program. NCT05487118.

titre: Immediate and 30-min effects of active versus passive scapular correction on clinical and sensorimotor outcomes in individuals with neck pain and scapular dysfunction: A double-blind, randomized, sham-controlled trial.
auteurs: Wannaprom Nipaporn, Maharan Sinthuporn, Ladawan Suphannika
revue: Journal of back and musculoskeletal rehabilitation
resume: BackgroundScapular correction has been demonstrated to improve pain, cervical range of motion (CROM), joint position error (JPE), and pressure pain threshold (PPT) in individuals with neck pain. However, whether active or passive scapular correction produces superior acute, short-term adaptations remains unknown.ObjectiveThe study aimed to investigate the immediate and 30-min follow-up effects of active and passive scapular correction, compared to sham control, on pain, CROM, JPEs, and PPTs in people with neck pain and scapular dysfunction.MethodsIn this double-blind randomized controlled trial, seventy-eight participants with neck pain and scapular dysfunction were randomly allocated to active, passive, or sham scapular correction. Each intervention consisted of 10 repetitions of 10 s: active self-correction in the active group, physiotherapist-performed passive correction in the passive group, or gentle touch in the sham group. Pain, CROM, JPEs, and PPTs were assessed at baseline, immediately post-intervention, and at 30-min follow-up.ResultsImmediately post-intervention, both active and passive groups demonstrated reduced pain intensity and increased CROM and PPTs compared to the sham group (all p < 0.05). At 30-min follow-up, these improvements were maintained only in the active group (all p < 0.05). Reductions in cervical and shoulder JPEs were observed only in the active group immediately post-intervention (all p < 0.05).ConclusionBoth active and passive scapular correction effectively improved pain intensity, cervical mobility and pain sensitivity immediately after intervention. However, active scapular correction may provide greater benefits by maintaining these effects at 30-min post-intervention and immediately improving joint position sense.

titre: Association of Early Stepwise Rehabilitation Nursing with Wrist Function and Pain Outcomes After Wrist Arthroscopy: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
auteurs: Men Lili, Liu Xin, Wei Lulu, Zhao Wei, Xu Pengcheng, Wu Xing
resume: Wrist arthroscopy is widely used as a minimally invasive treatment for wrist disorders. Postoperative rehabilitation is an important component of functional recovery. Conventional rehabilitation often follows a relatively uniform schedule and relies primarily on pharmacological pain management; consequently, stage-specific and individual needs may not be fully addressed. This single-center retrospective cohort analysis compared observed postoperative outcomes between patients receiving early stepwise rehabilitation care and those receiving the traditional rehabilitation model. The intervention group (n = 94) adopted a phased rehabilitation plan in which training intensity was dynamically adjusted according to the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), with additional physical therapy, psychological support, and family participation. The conventional group received conventional rehabilitation. At 3 and 6 months postoperatively, the intervention group showed higher Modified Mayo Wrist Score (MMWS), greater range of motion (ROM), stronger grip strength, and lower NRS scores than the conventional group (P < 0.001). Postrehabilitation complications were numerically less frequent in the intervention group than in the conventional group, but the difference was not statistically significant (6.4% vs. 15.3%, P = 0.080). The intervention group also showed higher postrehabilitation sensory conduction velocity (SCV), motor conduction velocity (MCV), and sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) amplitude, shorter two-point discrimination distance, lower Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS) and Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) scores, higher rehabilitation compliance, and higher satisfaction than the conventional group (P < 0.05). Early stepwise rehabilitation was associated with more favorable functional, pain, neurophysiological, sensory, psychological, adherence, and satisfaction outcomes; however, given the single-center retrospective design and non-random treatment allocation, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than evidence of causal effectiveness.

titre: Effects of Intrinsic Feedback-Based Gait Training Under Visual Deprivation on Balance and Gait in Stroke Survivors: A Randomized Controlled Study.
auteurs: Cho Myunggi
resume: Feedback is an essential component of motor learning and rehabilitation. Although extrinsic feedback is widely used in stroke rehabilitation, excessive dependence on external cues may limit opportunities for independent movement regulation. Training that emphasizes intrinsic feedback during visual deprivation (VD) may provide individuals with greater opportunities to perceive and regulate their movements using internally available sensory information. This study investigated the effects of gait training with intrinsic feedback on balance and gait abilities in individuals with stroke compared with extrinsic feedback training and conventional physical therapy. Thirty-six individuals with stroke were randomly assigned to the gait training with intrinsic feedback (GIF) group, gait training with extrinsic feedback (GEF) group, or control group (CG). The GIF performed forward and backward linear and curvilinear gait tasks on stable and unstable surfaces during VD without continuous verbal guidance. The GEF performed the same gait tasks during VD while receiving continuous verbal guidance, whereas the CG received conventional physical therapy. All interventions were conducted for 30 min, five times per week, for 8 weeks. Outcome measures included the Four Square Step Test (FSST), weight distribution, spatiotemporal gait variables, center of pressure (COP) variables, and the 10-Meter Walk Test (10 MWT). Significant group × time interactions were observed for the FSST, weight distribution, gait velocity, cadence, paretic stance phase, paretic swing phase, paretic step time, stride time, and the 10 MWT (p < 0.05). The GIF demonstrated significantly greater improvements than both the GEF and CG in the FSST, gait velocity, cadence, paretic step time, stride time, and the 10 MWT (p < 0.05). The GIF also showed greater improvement than the CG in weight distribution (p < 0.05). These findings suggest that gait training emphasizing intrinsic feedback during VD may provide additional benefits for selected aspects of balance and gait performance in individuals with stroke.

titre: Platelet-Rich Plasma as an Adjunct to Rehabilitation for Partial Rotator Cuff Tears in Recreational Athletes: A Comparative Study.
auteurs: Nair Ayyappan V, Mysore Shishir, Rajan Aravind, Reddy Harikanth, Priyamvada M, Khan Prince Shanavas
resume: The role of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) in the treatment of partial rotator cuff tears (RCTs) in young recreational athletes remains controversial. Our study aimed to investigate the efficacy and return-to-sports (RTS) rates of two commonly prescribed treatment options for partial RCTs in young recreational athletes. Sixty-one young recreational athletes with partial RCT were assigned based on patient preference to two groups: Physical therapy (PT) group (28 patients) receiving a standardized rehabilitation program and PRP with PT group (33 patients) receiving ultrasound-guided PRP injection at the site of the tear along with the same rehabilitation program. Functional outcomes such as the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score, Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, Hand (DASH) score, Constant-Murley score, and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) score were assessed at baseline and after 6 months. At 6 months, the PRP with PT group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in functional outcomes compared to the PT group. Adjusted Constant-Murley (89.4 vs. 79.5; P < 0.001) and ASES scores (83.7 vs. 75.2; P < 0.001) were higher in the PRP with PT group, while QuickDASH scores (48.8 vs. 24.5; P < 0.001) showed a steeper adjusted decline, indicating superior recovery of shoulder function in the PRP with PT group. However, after adjusting for baseline, VAS scores did not differ significantly between groups. RTS rates were 50% in the PRP with PT group versus 20% in the PT group (P < 0.05). Autologous PRP injection among recreational athletes with partial RCTs is an effective tool to be used as an adjunct to rehabilitation owing to its effect on improving shoulder function, reducing disability, and allowing greater rates of RTS.

titre: Conceptual Overlap Between OPTIMAL Theory Constructs and Motor Presentations in Functional Neurological Disorder Rehabilitation.
auteurs: Maggio Julie, Salon Heather, Hershberg Julie
revue: Journal of neurologic physical therapy : JNPT
resume: Functional neurological disorder (FND) is increasingly recognized as a disorder of brain network dysfunction with neuroimaging studies demonstrating altered communication among neural circuits involved in movement, attention, and self-agency. The Optimizing Performance Through Intrinsic Motivation and Attention for Learning (OPTIMAL) theory of motor learning is centered on the three constructs: external focus of attention, enhanced expectancies, and autonomy. This article explores the potential alignment between the pathophysiology underlying FND and the constructs proposed by the OPTIMAL theory and hypothesizes that OPTIMAL offers a promising, pathophysiology-informed framework for the physical therapy management of FND across varied practice settings. • FND is characterized by disrupted brain network communication, particularly in circuits related to motor learning, attention, and self-agency.• Physical therapy is supported by evidence as a first-line treatment for motor symptoms in FND; however, existing consensus guidelines do not identify an explicit motor learning framework to guide PT intervention• The OPTIMAL theory of motor learning emphasizes external focus of attention, enhanced expectancies, and autonomy, constructs that align with the neural networks implicated in FND and have demonstrated efficacy to improve motor learning when applied to healthy and neurological populations. • Applying motor learning constructs from OPTIMAL offers a practical and evidence-aligned approach to treating motor learning deficits in FND across care settings and age groups.• Therapists may improve motor outcomes in FND by incorporating external cueing, success-oriented feedback, and patient choice.

titre: Physiotherapist-delivered stress inoculation training integrated with exercise is cost-effective from a health system perspective compared with exercise alone for acute whiplash injury: an economic evaluation.
auteurs: Papic Christopher, Armfield Nigel, Elphinston Rachel A, Sterling Michele
resume: Is a physiotherapist-delivered integrated psychological and exercise intervention cost-effective compared with exercise alone for acute whiplash-associated disorders (WAD)? Economic evaluation using randomised controlled trial data, from health system (direct costs) and societal (direct and indirect costs) perspectives. Adults recruited from physiotherapy clinics, with acute WAD (< 4 weeks) and at least moderate neck pain-related disability and stress-related symptoms. Integrated stress inoculation training and exercise (StressModex) compared with exercise alone, both delivered by physiotherapists (10 sessions over 6 weeks). Both groups received an education booklet. Quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and Neck Disability Index (NDI; 0 to 100) over 12 months. Direct costs comprised physiotherapist training and patient healthcare utilisation; indirect costs were estimated from lost work productivity. Per participant, health system costs were AUD -290 (95% CI -1,168 to 570), with greater health gains for StressModex versus exercise alone (QALYs 0.07, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.15; NDI -8.7, 95% CI -14.3 to -3.1). From a health system perspective there was high probability of cost-effectiveness (90% at a willingness-to-pay of ∼ AUD 6,000 per QALY), with StressModex saving AUD 4,143 per QALY and AUD 330 per 10-point mean improvement in NDI. Societal costs were AUD 3,489 (95% CI -6,222 to 14,242) higher per participant for StressModex. The point-estimate ICERs (AUD 49,843 per QALY gained; AUD 4,200 per 10-point mean improvement in NDI) were within common Australian willingness-to-pay thresholds, but the probability of cost-effectiveness was modest (53% at AUD 60,000 per QALY). Compared with exercise alone, StressModex was cost-effective with high probability from a health system perspective. From a societal perspective, the point-estimate ICER fell within commonly used Australian willingness-to-pay thresholds, but with considerable uncertainty. Findings provide evidence to inform clinicians, insurers and policymakers on early intervention for acute WAD. ACTRN12614001036606.

titre: Addressing Physical Therapy Access Gaps: Impact of Embedded Scheduling Tools on Patient Language Preference.
auteurs: Pak Sang S, Jiang Yuxi, Raghunathan Harini, Bhide Heather, Auerbach Andrew
resume: Patients with Non-English language preference (NELP) face barriers accessing outpatient rehabilitation services, with disparities at the referral-to-scheduling stage. Despite decades of Federal mandates to provide meaningful access, patients with NELP remain operationally invisible in high-volume scheduling workflows, contributing to lower completion rates and delays compared to patients identified as English-proficient (EP). The objective was to evaluate whether implementing an electronic health record (EHR)-integrated language filter and visible language preference field improves referral scheduling for patients with NELP. This was a quasi-experimental study using interrupted time-series analysis. This study took place in outpatient rehabilitation clinics at an urban academic medical center. We studied 19,260 physical therapy referrals, including 985 (5.1%) patients with NELP and 18,275 (94.9%) patients with EP, from September 2024 to May 2025. We used a sortable "Preferred Language" field and toggle filter in the EHR referral workqueue enabling schedulers to identify and proactively schedule patients with NELP. Our primary outcome was the proportion of referrals scheduled within 10 days of referral. Secondary outcomes included overall scheduling rates, time from referral to scheduling, scheduling to visit, and referral to visit; no-show and unscheduled referral rates; and Press Ganey patient satisfaction scores related to appointment scheduling. Patients with NELP demonstrated a larger increase in the likelihood of scheduling within 10 days following the intervention (adjusted RL = 2.86, 95% CI = 1.82-4.48) relative to patients with EP. Scheduling within 10 days improved from 27.4% to 31.3% pre- and post-intervention. However, baseline disparities persisted, with patients with NELP experiencing a longer median time to scheduling throughout the study period (7 days vs 6 days). Implementation fidelity varied, with 22% of schedulers regularly using the tool. An EHR-integrated language visibility intervention improved 10-day scheduling rates among patients with NELP (adjusted RL = 2.86), yet baseline disparities persisted. Low implementation fidelity suggests that visibility intervention requires pairing with capacity enhancement and accountability structures for sustained, equitable access to rehabilitation services. Language-visibility EHR tools improve but do not eliminate scheduling disparities, pointing to the need for implementation infrastructure alongside technical solutions.

Language-visibility EHR tools improve but do not eliminate scheduling disparities, pointing to the need for implementation infrastructure alongside technical solutions.

titre: Extreme Diagnostic and Therapeutic Heterogeneity Limits Treatment Conclusions in Iliotibial Band Syndrome: A Systematic Review with Level-of-Evidence Stratification.
auteurs: Ferrero Andrea, Moro Alex, Minelli Marco, Marcolin Maria Giulia, Conte Pietro, Patrucco Francesco, D'Arrigo Daniele, Kon Elizaveta, Anzillotti Giuseppe
resume: Iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS) is a leading cause of lateral knee pain in runners and endurance athletes, yet clinical decision-making remains inconsistent and largely unsupported by high-quality comparative evidence. No comprehensive synthesis has previously integrated all available treatment modalities using a standardized evidence framework, and the evidence base for individual injection-based therapies continues to evolve rapidly. To evaluate all available treatment strategies for ITBS and stratify their efficacy according to the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (CEBM) levels of evidence. A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261374567) on 20 April 2026. PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 29 April 2026. Screening, data extraction, and the subsequent review processes were completed by 21 May 2026. An updated search subsequently identified one further eligible trial, published after the original cut-off. Eligible studies included RCTs, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, and case series reporting outcomes in adults with clinically diagnosed ITBS. Studies were classified into five treatment categories: therapeutic exercise, instrumental physical therapy, manual therapy and minimally invasive techniques, injection-based, pharmacological and biologic treatments, and surgical interventions. The primary outcomes were pain reduction and functional improvement; secondary outcomes included return to sport, recurrence, quality of life, patient satisfaction, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool and NIH Quality Assessment Tools. Twenty-four studies involving 1012 patients were included. Improvements in pain and function were reported across all treatment categories. Manual therapy, corticosteroid/pharmacological injections, and platelet-rich plasma reached Level I evidence; therapeutic exercise and instrumental physical therapy Level Ib; surgical treatments Level IV. A single, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trial now provides Level I evidence for ultrasound-guided platelet-rich plasma (PRP) in refractory ITBS, whereas TECAR (Transfer of Energy Capacitive And Resistive), low-level laser, prolotherapy, and hyaluronic acid still lacked any ITBS-specific controlled evidence. Despite a broad therapeutic landscape, most treatment modalities cannot yet be recommended over one another. Structured rehabilitation remains the reasonable first-line approach for newly diagnosed ITBS. For refractory ITBS, emerging Level I evidence supports ultrasound-guided PRP as a promising, though not yet independently replicated, minimally invasive option; corticosteroid injection, instrumental therapies and surgery may be considered in selected cases. The absence of standardized diagnostic criteria and extreme methodological heterogeneity across studies - rather than limitations of this review - preclude more definitive conclusions. Future research must prioritize diagnostic standardization and rigorous head-to-head comparative trials, including independent replication of the PRP findings.

titre: Exercise training in adults with neuromuscular diseases: insights from two global surveys of lived experience and clinical practice.
auteurs: Poulsen Nanna Scharff, Kroneman Madelon, de Groot Ingrid, Oorschot Sander, Bustos-Sellers Asunción, van Esch Charlotte, Lucia Alejandro, Vissing John, Voorn Eric Lukas
resume: Regular exercise may improve health and reduce morbidity in people with neuromuscular diseases. This study examined the application of exercise, perceived barriers to it, perceived benefits from it, and the support needs of healthcare professionals and adults with neuromuscular diseases. Two international online surveys were distributed through professional networks, patient organizations, and social media. A survey for healthcare professionals was open, from August-November 2024. It was answered by 109 respondents from 19 countries across three continents covering respondent profile, prescription practice, perceived barriers, and need for support. A patient survey was open from July-September 2024. It had a response of 1909 adult respondents from 42 countries across six continents covering respondent profiles, engagement in exercise, perceived barriers, and benefits. Although 80% of people with neuromuscular diseases reported engaging in exercise and 94% of healthcare professionals reported prescribing exercise, these estimates are likely influenced by non-response bias. Despite this, 77% of healthcare professionals reported underuse (i.e., insufficient training dose), suggesting that exercise is perceived as not being fully implemented in clinical practice. Aerobic exercise was typically prescribed thrice weekly at moderate intensity for 21-30 minutes, while resistance training was commonly prescribed twice weekly at low-to-moderate intensity for 11-20 minutes. Reported exercise patterns in both surveys were broadly consistent with recent recommendations. Barriers were multifactorial. Healthcare professionals most frequently reported safety concerns, lack of guidelines, and insufficient staff, whereas people with neuromuscular diseases reported health-related concerns and low motivation. People not exercising reported barriers more frequently than people who exercised, and wheelchair use was associated with lower odds of exercise engagement and more barriers. Although exercise is commonly prescribed and widely perceived as beneficial, underuse and barriers remain. Development of personalized guidelines addressing safety, individual motivators, and barriers may support greater exercise participation in adults with neuromuscular diseases.

titre: Neural mobilization in cervicogenic headache: a scoping review of current evidence.
auteurs: Vaid Nikita, Saxena Akanksha, Jangra Mandeep Kumar
revue: The Journal of manual & manipulative therapy
resume: Neural mobilization has increasingly been incorporated into physiotherapy management for cervicogenic headache (CGH); however, evidence regarding its clinical effectiveness remains limited. This scoping review aimed to explore and map the existing evidence on neural mobilization in the management of CGH, with emphasis on pain, headache-related disability, and functional outcomes. A scoping review was conducted using PubMed (MEDLINE), PEDro, ScienceDirect, and the Cochrane Library to identify studies involving adults with CGH receiving neural mobilization or neurodynamic interventions. Outcomes assessed included pain, headache frequency, disability, cervical posture, and quality of life. From 699 identified records, five studies comprising one pilot randomized controlled trial, two comparative clinical studies, and two case reports involving 142 participants were included in the review. Across the included studies, interventions incorporating neural mobilization were associated with improvements in pain intensity, headache frequency, headache-related disability, cervical posture, cervical range of motion, and quality of life. Neural mobilization was predominantly delivered as part of multimodal physiotherapy programs, particularly alongside postural correction and other physiotherapy interventions. However, the evidence was limited by the small number of studies, methodological heterogeneity, variation in neural mobilization protocols, and limited long-term follow-up. Current evidence indicates that neural mobilization is a promising adjunct within multimodal physiotherapy management of CGH. However, the available evidence is insufficient to establish its independent therapeutic effectiveness. Further well-designed studies using standardized neural mobilization protocols, appropriate comparator groups, and longer follow-up are required to strengthen the evidence base.

titre: [Surgical Treatment of Lumbar Spine Lesions: Collaboration with Neurologists from an Orthopedic Surgeon's Perspective].
auteurs: Inoue Hirokazu, Takeshita Katsushi
revue: Brain and nerve = Shinkei kenkyu no shinpo
resume: Surgical indications for lumbar spine disorders should not be determined solely based on degenerative or stenotic magnetic resonance imaging findings. This article discusses how orthopedic spine surgeons evaluate lumbar pathology in collaboration with neurologists. The central issue is whether the patient's symptoms, neurological findings, and imaging abnormalities can be used to identify the responsible lesion that is likely to improve after surgery. Differential diagnoses, including cervical or thoracic myelopathy, peripheral neuropathy, motor neuron disease, vascular claudication, hip disease, tumors, and infection, must be considered, particularly in older patients with multiple coexisting disorders. The article also outlines orthopedic perspectives that influence surgical decision-making, including spinal instability, sagittal and coronal alignment, bone quality, frailty, sarcopenia, walking ability, and postoperative activities of daily living. The choice between decompression alone and decompression with fusion was reviewed together with perioperative management, rehabilitation, patient explanation, and shared decision-making. Complementary collaboration between orthopedic surgeons and neurologists may help clarify the responsible lesion, optimize referral timing, and avoid undertreatment and overtreatment.

titre: Gait Retraining for Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome: A Biomechanical Approach to Pain Relief and Performance Optimization.
auteurs: Tedeschi Roberto, Giorgi Federica
revue: Clinical journal of sport medicine : official journal of the Canadian Academy of Sport Medicine
resume: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is common among runners and is linked to biomechanical dysfunctions that increase patellofemoral joint stress. Gait retraining has been proposed to redistribute this loading, but the effectiveness of different retraining strategies and their long-term impact remain unclear. This scoping review synthesizes existing evidence on gait retraining strategies for PFPS, focusing on pain, function, and biomechanics. MEDLINE, Cochrane CENTRAL, Scopus, PEDro, and Web of Science were searched, following the methodological framework of the Joanna Briggs Institute for scoping reviews. Studies investigating gait retraining interventions in runners diagnosed with PFPS were included. Key outcomes were pain reduction, functional improvement, biomechanical adaptations, and adverse effects. Three randomized controlled trials met the inclusion criteria, examining cadence modification, impact reduction, and foot strike adjustments. Intervention groups experienced significant pain reduction, with Visual Analog Scale scores improving by 2 to 4 points, alongside functional gains reflected by increased Kujala and Knee Outcome Survey of the Activities of Daily Living Scale scores. Biomechanical adaptations included decreased patellofemoral joint stress, lower impact forces, and improved load distribution. Some participants reported transient calf discomfort during the adaptation period, which resolved over time. Gait retraining is an effective intervention for runners with PFPS, showing sustained pain relief, functional improvement, and biomechanical benefits. Individualized protocols and gradual implementation are essential to optimize outcomes and minimize discomfort. Future research should address long-term retention of gait modifications, optimal training parameters, and applicability beyond runners.

titre: Polypharmacy and Activities of Daily Living in Older Patients Undergoing Cerebrovascular Rehabilitation: An Observational Study Using Japanese Real-World Data.
auteurs: Ogawa Yukari, Horii Takeshi, Sakoh Masaharu, Mihara Kiyoshi
resume: Polypharmacy is highly prevalent among older patients undergoing cerebrovascular rehabilitation and may adversely affect functional recovery. This study examined the association between polypharmacy and the extent and pace of functional recovery in older patients undergoing convalescent rehabilitation after cerebrovascular events. This retrospective observational study used a Japanese real-world claims database (Japan Medical Data Center claims database, accessed on 25 August 2025), and included patients aged ≥ 65 years admitted to convalescent rehabilitation wards for cerebrovascular diseases. Polypharmacy was defined as the use of six or more medications. Patients were categorized into four groups according to polypharmacy status at admission and discharge: persistent non-polypharmacy, polypharmacy resolved, incident polypharmacy, and persistent polypharmacy. Functional outcomes were assessed using the Functional Independence Measure (FIM). The primary outcome measure was FIM gain, and the secondary outcome measure was FIM efficiency. Multivariable linear regression analyses adjusted for patient characteristics, comorbidities, and hospital bed capacity were performed. Among 44,980 patients, 48.9% had persistent polypharmacy and 14.8% developed incident polypharmacy during hospitalization. Polypharmacy status was not significantly associated with FIM gain. In contrast, FIM efficiency was significantly lower in the polypharmacy-resolved, incident polypharmacy, and persistent polypharmacy groups than in the persistent non-polypharmacy group. The strongest negative association with FIM efficiency was observed in the incident polypharmacy group (B = -0.114, p < 0.001), followed by the persistent polypharmacy group (B = -0.069, p < 0.001). Polypharmacy status was not significantly associated with FIM gain, the primary outcome. Although the three polypharmacy groups had lower FIM efficiency and longer hospital stays than the persistent non-polypharmacy group, the lower FIM efficiency may partly reflect differences in length of hospital stay. These observational findings do not establish a causal relationship between changes in medication burden and functional recovery.

titre: Neuromuscular, Balance, and Gait Factors Associated with Falls and Fall-Related Outcomes in Individuals with COPD: A Systematic Review.
auteurs: Zangi Mahsa, Shamsi Hasan, Rahmani Rasa Amir, Mirsaeidi Hannaneh, Nemati Aysan, Khosravi Mobina
revue: International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
resume: Individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have a higher incidence of falls than age-matched peers, which may result in injury, loss of independence, and reduced quality of life. Although falls have often been attributed to general deconditioning, impairments in muscle strength, balance, and gait may also contribute. This systematic review synthesized evidence on the relationships between these factors and falls or fall-related outcomes in people with COPD. PubMed, Web of Knowledge, Scopus and Google Scholar were searched for English-language studies published up to November 2024. Twenty-five original studies involving 1295 participants met the inclusion criteria. Methodological quality was assessed using a modified Downs and Black checklist. Seventeen of the 25 studies reported a significant association between at least one examined factor and fall history or fall risk. Balance impairment showed the most consistent relationship, with positive associations reported in 14 of 17 studies. Evidence regarding muscle strength was mixed: some studies linked quadriceps weakness to increased fall risk, including one reporting an odds ratio of 2.9, whereas others found no significant association. Altered gait characteristics, particularly increased step-time variability, were also associated with falls. Balance and gait impairments are consistently associated with falls and fall-related outcomes in individuals with COPD, whereas the relationship with muscle strength is less consistent. Given the predominance of observational studies, prospective research and controlled trials are needed to clarify causal pathways and determine whether targeted balance and strength training can reduce fall risk as part of pulmonary rehabilitation.

titre: Sociodemographic and clinical factors associated with seven domains of digital health literacy: A cross-sectional study (NORFAST).
auteurs: Linnestad Anne-Margrethe, Larsen Marie Hamilton, Gay Caryl L, Skogestad Ingrid Johansen, Indredavik Bent, Stubberud Jan, Lerdal Anners
resume: Introduction Due to limited digital health literacy (DHL), stroke survivors frequently face barriers in using digital health tools essential for post-stroke rehabilitation and self-management. DHL is a multidimensional construct, encompassing several distinct skill domains. Although sociodemographic and clinical characteristics may influence overall DHL, their associations with specific DHL domains remain poorly understood. This study therefore explores how individual DHL domains relate to patient characteristics in stroke survivors. Methods In this cross-sectional NORFAST study, stroke survivors aged 18-80 years with a first-ever stroke in 2021 or 2022 were recruited through the Norwegian Stroke Registry. Registry data included diagnosis, stroke type, aphasia, and scores on the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), modified Rankin Scale (mRS), and Barthel Index for Activities of Daily Living. Cognitive function was assessed before inclusion using the Mini/5min MoCA, a brief telephone-administered cognitive screening tool. Participants also completed self-report questionnaires (telephone or electronic), assessing sociodemographics, self-rated health status (EQ-VAS) and fatigue interference (Fatigue Severity Scale, FSS-7). The primary outcomes were DHL dimensions, assessed with the 7-domain eHealth Literacy Questionnaire (eHLQ). Linear regression models examined unadjusted and adjusted associations between patient characteristics and each DHL domain. Results Among 177 stroke survivors (mean age 69), most had experienced minor strokes and cerebral infarction. Patients scored highest on the domain "feel safe and in control", and lowest on "digital services that suit individual needs". In multivariable regression models, older age was associated with lower scores on Using technology, Engage, Motivation, and Needs; female sex with lower scores on Motivation and Needs; college/university education with higher scores on Understanding, Engage, Motivation and Needs; and better health status with higher scores on domains Using technology, Understanding, Motivation, Access and Needs. Living alone, aphasia, cognitive function, and fatigue interference were not significantly associated with any DHL domain after multivariable adjustment. Conclusion This study demonstrates considerable variation in DHL across domains among stroke survivors. After adjustment, age, education level, and self-rated health status were the factors most consistently associated with DHL dimensions. These findings suggest that older stroke survivors, those without college or university education, and those with lower self-rated health may warrant particular attention when designing, implementing, and evaluating digital health interventions. Co-creation with stroke survivors, healthcare professionals, and technology designers may support the development of accessible and clinically meaningful digital solutions.

titre: Gua Sha (Scraping Therapy) for Spasticity After Stroke: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of RCTs with Integrated Preclinical Mechanistic Synthesis.
auteurs: Li Fei, Wang Jun-Xiang, Zhong Jin-Shan, Tian Shi-Jing-Xin, Li Xiang
resume: ​Emerging clinical data from Chinese randomized controlled trials (RCTs) suggest Gua Sha (scraping therapy) may deliver adjunct antispastic benefits for spasticity after stroke (SAS) when combined with standard rehabilitation. This study aimed to synthesize clinical efficacy evidence and explore treatment parameters for this intervention. We searched eight electronic databases from database inception to January 1, 2026; two independent reviewers completed study screening, risk-of-bias assessment using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool, and data extraction. Meta-analytic effect sizes were calculated using mean difference (MD), and the review protocol was preregistered on PROSPERO. Sixteen eligible RCTs enrolling 1227 stroke survivors were included, all conducted in China, which may limit the external transferability of our results. Pooled random-effects estimates indicated that add-on scraping therapy was associated with reduced Modified Ashworth Scale and Visual Analog Scale for Pain (VAS-P) scores, lower serum hs-CRP and Hcy, as well as improved motor function and activities of daily living. Grading of Recommendations Assessment (GRADE) rated the certainty of evidence for all outcomes as very low due to high heterogeneity, methodological limitations, suspected publication bias and limited cross-regional data. Exploratory subgroup analyses identified numerically larger spasticity relief in regimens with 5-day treatment intervals, 1.5-month treatment duration and intensive scraping stimulation. These cross-study comparisons generate preliminary hypotheses awaiting verification through dedicated head-to-head dosing trials. Proposed mechanistic pathways linking scraping therapy to symptom relief rely largely on preclinical evidence, including enhanced local microcirculation and modulation of inflammatory and neural signaling. Current evidence supports scraping therapy as an investigational adjunctive strategy for SAS. Given the low-certainty evidence base and lack of inclusion in international rehabilitation guidelines, this therapy should be evaluated only in clinical settings with certified practitioners and standardized adverse event monitoring. Further well-designed RCTs are required to clarify its long-term therapeutic benefits and complete safety profile.

titre_fr: Gua Sha (Scraping Therapy) for Spasticity After Stroke: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of RCTs with Integrated Preclinical Mechanistic Synthesis.
resume_fr: ​Emerging clinical data from Chinese randomized controlled trials (RCTs) suggest Gua Sha (scraping therapy) may deliver adjunct antispastic benefits for spasticity after stroke (SAS) when combined with standard rehabilitation. This study aimed to synthesize clinical efficacy evidence and explore treatment parameters for this intervention. We searched eight electronic databases from database inception to January 1, 2026; two independent reviewers completed study screening, risk-of-bias assessment using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool, and data extraction. Meta-analytic effect sizes were calculated using mean difference (MD), and the review protocol was preregistered on PROSPERO. Pooled random-effects estimates indicated that add-on scraping therapy was associated with reduced Modified Ashworth Scale and Visual Analog Scale for Pain (VAS-P) scores, lower serum hs-CRP and Hcy, as well as improved motor function and activities of daily living. Grading of Recommendations Assessment (GRADE) rated the certainty of evidence for all outcomes as very low due to high heterogeneity, methodological limitations, suspected publication bias and limited cross-regional data. Exploratory subgroup analyses identified numerically larger spasticity relief in regimens with 5-day treatment intervals, 1.5-month treatment duration and intensive scraping stimulation. These cross-study comparisons generate preliminary hypotheses awaiting verification through dedicated head-to-head dosing trials. Proposed mechanistic pathways linking scraping therapy to symptom relief rely largely on preclinical evidence, including enhanced local microcirculation and modulation of inflammatory and neural signaling. Current evidence supports scraping therapy as an investigational adjunctive strategy for SAS. titre: The effect of video-based games on upper extremity function and activity participation in children with hemiparetic cerebral palsy.
auteurs: Şen Tekin Şengül, Yarar Feride
resume: Upper extremity dysfunction and limited participation in daily activities are common in children with hemiparetic cerebral palsy and may restrict independence and social engagement. Interactive video-based rehabilitation has emerged as a promising adjunct to conventional therapy. This study aimed to evaluate whether motion-detection video games (Microsoft Xbox Kinect) combined with neurodevelopmental therapy (NDT) provide additional benefits in upper extremity function and activity participation compared with NDT alone. This randomized controlled study included children aged 7-13 years with hemiparetic cerebral palsy classified as Levels I-III according to the Gross Motor Function Classification System and Levels 1-3 on the Manual Ability Classification System. Participants were randomly assigned to an intervention group receiving combined NDT and video-game-based training or a control group receiving only NDT for 12 weeks. The study was conducted at Özel İlk Yankı Special Education and Rehabilitation Center. Outcomes included hand function assessed by the Nine-Hole Peg Test (9HPT) and Duruöz Hand Index (DHI), and activity participation assessed by the Assistance to Participation Scale (APS). Assessments were performed at baseline and post-intervention by a blinded physiotherapist. Data were analyzed using parametric tests, and effect sizes were calculated. . A total of 24 participants completed the study (n = 12 per group). Both groups demonstrated significant within-group improvements in APS, DHI, and 9HPT scores (p < .05). Between-group comparisons revealed significantly greater improvements in the intervention group for APS (p = .043) and DHI (p = .049), with large effect sizes (d = 0.87 and d = 0.84, respectively). No statistically significant between-group difference was observed for 9HPT (p = .096), although a moderate effect size (d = 0.71) was detected. The addition of video-based gaming to conventional NDT may provide additional benefits in functional hand use and activity participation in children with hemiparetic cerebral palsy when delivered within a matched therapy dosage framework. Although no significant between-group difference was observed in fine motor performance, the moderate effect size suggests a potential effect that may not have reached statistical significance. Video-based gaming may be considered a feasible complementary approach in pediatric neurorehabilitation; however, further studies with larger sample sizes and long-term follow-up are warranted. titre: Jue Tone Music Therapy for Post-stroke Depression in China: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
auteurs: Jin Yan, Qian Yan-Na, Zhu Bing-Jun
revue: International journal of psychiatry in medicine
resume: ObjectiveTo evaluate the effects of Jue tone music therapy on depressive symptoms, sleep quality, activities of daily living, and selected serum biomarkers in patients with post-stroke depression (PSD).MethodsIn this randomized controlled trial, patients with PSD were randomly assigned to a control group or an intervention group. The control group received usual care, including sertraline hydrochloride and comprehensive rehabilitation training. The intervention group received additional Jue tone music therapy based on Five Element Music Therapy for 6 weeks. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the 24-item Hamilton Depression Scale (HAMD-24) and the depression subscale of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS-D). Sleep quality and activities of daily living were evaluated using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Barthel Index (BI). Serum interleukin-6 (IL-6), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) levels were measured before and after the intervention.ResultsA total of 91 patients completed the study (control group, n = 46; intervention group, n = 45). After 6 weeks, the intervention group showed significantly lower HAMD-24, HADS-D, and PSQI scores and higher BI scores compared with the control group (all P < 0.01). Serum IL-6 levels were significantly reduced, while BDNF and 5-HT levels were significantly increased in the intervention group (all P < 0.05). No significant differences in adverse events were observed between groups.ConclusionJue tone music therapy is a safe and effective adjunct to usual care, improving depressive symptoms, sleep quality, and functional outcomes in patients with PSD.

titre: Visual Feedback-Based Rehabilitation Improves Gait Recovery After Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial.
auteurs: Spanò Riccardo, Ammendolia Antonio, Marotta Nicola, de Sire Alessandro, Raso Maria Girolama, Carozzo Simone
resume: This randomized controlled trial investigated whether adding a visual feedback-based (VFB) rehabilitation program to standard care could enhance gait performance and pelvic kinematics in patients recovering from total hip arthroplasty (THA). Inpatients aged 55 to 80 years who underwent unilateral THA by a lateral approach were randomized to either a VFB group or a control group. The VFB group received 30 minutes of technology-assisted visual feedback training using TecnoBody systems plus 30 minutes of conventional physiotherapy daily, while the control group received one hour of conventional therapy alone, both 5 days per week for 6 weeks. Gait and pelvic kinematics were assessed using the G-WALK inertial sensor at baseline and after 6 weeks, alongside clinical measures for pain, functional independence, and ambulation capacity. Both groups showed significant improvements on clinical scales, with no meaningful differences between them. However, the VFB group demonstrated significantly greater gains in key gait and kinematic parameters, including cadence, speed, symmetry, pelvic tilt, and pelvic obliquity, with multivariate analysis confirming a distinct and more favorable post-treatment kinematic profile. Incorporating visual feedback-based training into postoperative rehabilitation after THA leads to superior improvements in gait quality and pelvic control compared with conventional therapy alone, supporting its clinical integration in standard physiotherapy programs. Therapeutic Level I. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

titre: Game-oriented interventions for children with cerebral palsy: a review of efficacy, engagement, and functional outcomes.
auteurs: Mahmood Qamar
resume: Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most prevalent cause of childhood physical disability worldwide, affecting approximately 1.6 per 1,000 live births and imposing permanent deficits across motor, cognitive, and psychosocial domains. Conventional rehabilitation is frequently constrained by poor engagement and inadequate practice intensity in pediatric populations. Game-based interventions - encompassing virtual reality (VR), exergaming platforms, serious games, augmented reality, and telerehabilitation systems - address this challenge by embedding intensive therapeutic motor practice within intrinsically motivating play environments. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on the efficacy, engagement profiles, neuroplasticity mechanisms, and functional outcomes of game-oriented interventions for children with CP. A structured narrative synthesis was conducted using 25 peer-reviewed articles published between 2021 and 2025, identified through a structured literature search of Scopus and Web of Science. Eligible sources included systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, feasibility studies, and scoping reviews. Evidence was organized thematically around game technology types, functional outcome domains, neuroplastic mechanisms, and clinical implementation factors. Converging evidence demonstrates that game-based interventions produce statistically significant, though modest and not yet clinically validated, improvements in gross motor function (GMFM-88 MD = 0.81; 95% CI [0.15, 1.47]), alongside improvements of uncertain long-term durability in upper limb dexterity, balance, gait kinematics, and activities of daily living. VR-assisted exergaming shows a statistically greater improvement than conventional physiotherapy for GMFM walking and standing dimensions, though this has not been shown to reflect a dose-matched or clinically established advantage. Neuroimaging findings are associated with use-dependent cortical reorganization as a proposed neuroplastic mechanism; this evidence is predominantly correlational, and a causal or mediating role has not been directly demonstrated. Game-based interventions represent a scientifically grounded and clinically feasible modality for pediatric CP rehabilitation that directly addresses the engagement and intensity limitations of conventional therapy. Methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and insufficient long-term follow-up remain the primary evidence limitations. Future priorities include standardized outcome measurement, adaptive AI-driven game systems, and adequately powered telerehabilitation trials. Integration into routine neurorehabilitation practice is supported by the current evidence base.

titre: Blood Flow Restriction Training in Stroke Rehabilitation: A Narrative Review of Current Evidence and Future Directions.
auteurs: Tong Jiawei, Song Lei, Jin Juan, Li Fangfang, Huang Tao, Ying Hang, Zhu Jiawei, Wang Jue, Zhuang Jie
resume: Post-stroke motor deficits cause disability, while paresis and comorbidities may limit high-intensity training. Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) combines low-intensity exercise with partial vascular occlusion and may promote neuromuscular adaptations at low loads. This narrative review synthesized peer-reviewed evidence on BFRT in stroke rehabilitation. Stroke-specific clinical studies, particularly randomized controlled trials (RCTs), were prioritized for evaluating clinical effects; experimental, preclinical, physiological, mechanistic, review, and guideline evidence provided context. RCT data included participant characteristics, protocols, outcomes, and adverse events. Two reviewers independently assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB 1). Findings were synthesized qualitatively without meta-analysis or GRADE assessment. Sixty-seven reports were included, comprising eight stroke-specific clinical studies and 59 contextual reports. Participants represented early, subacute, and chronic stroke stages, although stroke stage and baseline impairment were inconsistently reported. Studies generally enrolled medically stable individuals with adequate motor control, postural stability, or walking capacity; those with severe paresis or substantial mobility dependence were underrepresented. Improvements were reported in strength, motor function, balance, walking, mobility, activities of daily living, muscle morphology, and cortical activation. However, between-group benefits were inconsistent, and BFRT was not consistently superior to conventional, unrestricted, or high-intensity resistance exercise. No serious BFRT-related adverse events were reported, but safety reporting was incomplete. BFRT may be a useful low-load adjunct for selected stroke survivors, particularly in lower-limb rehabilitation. Evidence remains preliminary because of risk of bias, small samples, heterogeneous protocols, short follow-up, and limited representation of severely impaired patients. Well-controlled studies are needed before broad implementation.

titre: First aggression as a planning signal in post-acute stroke rehabilitation: Service benchmarks, goal setting, and a 60-day precaution window from a comprehensive observational cohort.
auteurs: García-Rudolph Alejandro, Hernandez-Pena Elena, Romero Alicia, Wright Mark Andrew, Saurí Joan, Teixido-Font Claudia, Opisso Eloy, Cedersund Gunnar, Bernabeu Montserrat
revue: PM & R : the journal of injury, function, and rehabilitation
resume: Aggressive behavior after stroke is common and linked to poorer outcomes, yet prior studies have not translated this knowledge into operational benchmarks that guide planning (time-limited risk windows, realistic goals, discharge timelines) during postacute rehabilitation. To quantify service benchmarks after the first electronic health record (EHR)-documented aggression and map them to a standardized, time-boxed response: event rates and short-horizon risks (30/60 days), functional/length-of-stay (LOS) gaps in clinical units, and practical targets for planning. Retrospective observational cohort with prespecified 1:1 propensity-matched sensitivity analysis. Single tertiary neurorehabilitation hospital (postacute, inpatient). Adults with first-ever ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke admitted ≤3 months post stroke between 2005 and 2023 (N = 1683). Aggression was flagged at the first qualifying EHR annotation; 317 (18.8%) had more than one episode. Incidence densities (per 1000 patient-days) and derived 30-/60-day risks for first aggression, urinary tract infection, and falls; between-group differences in LOS and motor Functional Independence Measure (mFIM) outcomes (gain, efficiency, effectiveness) summarized as median differences (Hodges-Lehmann). Across 111,945 patient-days, first-aggression incidence was 2.83/1000 (95% CI: 2.53-3.16), implying 8.1% 30-day and 15.6% 60-day risks. Compared with nonaggressive patients, the aggressive group had higher urinary tract infection rates (rate ratio 1.92, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.43-2.57) and falls (rate ratio 1.28, 95% CI: 1.00-1.63). Functional gaps (median differences, Hodges-Lehmann) favored the nonaggressive group: LOS was longer (+17.9 days, 95% CI +13.8 to +22.0), mFIM efficiency and effectiveness were lower in the full cohort; in the matched subset (317 vs. 317), Hodges-Lehmann differences persisted (eg, LOS +9.8 days, 95% CI +4.1 to +15.2). A single EHR-documented aggression provides a planning signal: event rates and 30-/60-day risks justify a 60-day precaution window, and scaled gaps support realistic goal setting (mFIM) and discharge date updates. These benchmarks offer a framework for bedside counseling, service targets, and audit; multicenter validation is warranted.

titre: Barriers to early rehabilitation and mobilization in adult ICUs: A multicenter survey in the Eastern region of Saudi Arabia.
auteurs: Al Humoud Shoug Yousef, Alasmi Najlaa K, Alquaimi Maher M, Almojaibel Abdullah A, Alhassan Fatima H, Aljouf Maha M, Alsubaiei Mohammed S, Alghamdi Renad A, Raza Saqlain, Alzahrani Yahya H, Alsomali Hana, Al Asmari Mansour A, Alnoaimi Noorah
resume: Prolonged Intensive Care Unit (ICU) immobilization leads to complications such as ICU Acquired Weakness (ICU-AW). While Early Rehabilitation and Mobilization (ERM) is proven to improve functional independence and reduce mechanical ventilation (MV) duration, its implementation remains inconsistent. This study aimed to identify barriers to ERM as perceived by adult ICU healthcare practitioners in the Eastern region of Saudi Arabia. A multicenter, cross-sectional survey using a 21-question adapted self-administered questionnaire was conducted between January and April 2023 through QuestionPro platform. The survey was distributed to critical care practitioners including physicians, nurses, respiratory therapists, physiotherapists, and other allied health staff. Respondents represented three hospital categories in the Eastern region: private, Eastern Health Cluster, and other governmental sector hospitals. Barriers were assessed a priori at three levels: patient, provider, and institutional. Internal consistency of the patient-level barrier scale was assessed using Cronbach's alpha. Chi-square and Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact tests compared ERM protocol availability between hospital sectors and knowledge, practice, and resource variables across professional groups. Of 137 practitioners who accessed the survey, 121of 137 who accessed the link completed the questionnaire (88%completion rate). Although 66 (55%) rated ERM as very important, only 48 (40%) reported always participating in or observing it in practice. The most frequently endorsed ideal initiation time was within 24 hours of admission (38, 31%), whereas the most commonly reported actual initiation point was when patients were conscious and able to cooperate (28, 23%); only 10 (8%) reported initiation within 24 hours. Patient-level barriers were mainly sedation and physiological instability. Provider-level barriers included safety concerns, limited staffing, and inadequate training. At the institutional level, only 57 (47%) respondents reported the presence of a formal ERM protocol, with a significant difference between private hospitals (36/54, 67%) and government hospitals (21/67, 31%) (χ<sup>2</sup> = 13.59 df = 1, p < 0.001; OR 4.38, 95% CI 2.04-9.42). Protocol availability, ERM participation, and physiotherapy access also differed significantly across professional groups, with respiratory therapists consistently reporting the lowest access p = 0.013; p < 0.001; p = 0.038; p < 0.001. Despite high awareness of its benefits, ERM implementation across adult ICUs in the Eastern region remains suboptimal relative to the 72-hour initiation window recommended by current consensus guidance and is delivered reactively rather than proactively. Barriers operate at patient, provider, and institutional levels, and both formal ERM protocol availability and profession-based access to ERM structures differ significantly, with respiratory therapists the most excluded despite managing the highest-risk patients. These findings identify protocol availability and interdisciplinary delivery structures as the principal targets for regional implementation efforts.

Barriers operate at patient, provider, and institutional levels, and both formal ERM protocol availability and profession-based access to ERM structures differ significantly, with respiratory therapists the most excluded despite managing the highest-risk patients. These findings identify protocol availability and interdisciplinary delivery structures as the principal targets for regional implementation efforts.

titre: Effect of Integrated Respiratory and Functional Training on Weaning from Mechanical Ventilation, Respiratory and Peripheral Muscle Strength, Functional Ability, and Pain After Emergency Abdominal Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
auteurs: Mehani Sherin Hassan Mohammed, Mohamed Ayman A, Mohamed Mohamed Sayed, Mahmoud Mahmoud Ibrahim Mohamed
revue: Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation
resume: To compare the effects of integrated respiratory and functional (multidimensional functional) training versus high-intensity inspiratory muscle training (IMT) plus conventional chest physiotherapy (CPT) on ventilator weaning after emergency abdominal surgery. Prospective, multicenter, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial. Two intensive care units. Ninety mechanically ventilated patients with difficult weaning following emergency abdominal surgery (N=90). Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to the study group and control groups. The study group received multidimensional functional training, high-intensity IMT and conventional chest physiotherapy. The control group received high-intensity IMT and conventional chest physiotherapy. Primary outcomes were weaning success and maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP). Secondary outcomes included rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI), peripheral muscle strength, Functional Independence Measure (FIM), pain, weaning duration, and intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay. Weaning success was significantly higher in the study group (95.6% vs 82.2%; P = .044). Both groups significantly improved MIP, with no between-group difference after treatment (mean difference [MD]=0.30 cmH₂O; 95% confidence interval [CI], -4.11 to 4.72; P=0.89). Compared with control group, the study group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in all peripheral muscle strength measures and FIM domains (all P<0.001), greater reductions in RSBI (MD=-3.92 breaths/min/L; 95% CI, -6.85 to -1.00; P=0.01) and pain (MD=3.22; 95% CI, 3 to 3.44; P<0.001), and shorter weaning duration (MD=-5.82 days; 95% CI, -7.98 to -3.67; P<0.001) and ICU length of stay (MD=-7.74 days; 95% CI, -11.37 to -4.11; P<0.001). Both training approaches improved MIP, whereas multidimensional functional training resulted in higher weaning success and greater improvements in peripheral muscle strength, functional independence, pain, weaning duration, and ICU length of stay than high-intensity IMT+CPT in patients following emergency abdominal surgery.

titre: Investigation of the physical and emotional status of elderly individuals with and without COVID-19: a cross-sectional study.
auteurs: Mutlu Ali, Büyükturan Buket, Büyükturan Öznur
resume: This study aimed to compare balance, functional mobility, activities of daily living (ADLs), quality of life (QoL), fear of COVID-19, and depression between older adults with and without a history of COVID-19, and to explore the associations between physical and emotional outcomes in both groups. This observational cross-sectional study included 52 older adults with COVID-19 evaluated during the acute pre-discharge phase and 55 older adults without COVID-19 from the same region. Balance, functional mobility, ADLs, QoL, fear of COVID-19, and depression were assessed using validated measures. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Age-adjusted ANCOVA was conducted as a sensitivity analysis. Spearman correlations and Fisher's z comparisons examined group-specific associations. Older adults with COVID-19 had poorer balance, functional mobility, and ADLs independence, lower QoL, and higher fear of COVID-19 and depression than controls. These differences remained significant after age adjustment. In the COVID-19 group, fear of COVID-19 and depression were associated with poorer functional mobility, lower balance scores, and lower ADLs independence. Fear of COVID-19 was not associated with physical function in controls. Fisher's z comparisons showed stronger negative associations of depression with functional mobility and ADLs independence in the COVID-19 group. Older adults recovering from COVID-19 showed coexisting physical and emotional impairments. Physical function and emotional status, particularly depression, functional mobility, and ADLs independence, appear interrelated. Rehabilitation and nursing care should address both physical and psychosocial needs to support functional independence and reintegration into daily life after COVID-19 or similar acute health events.

titre: Dose-response effects of robot-assisted training on poststroke functional recovery: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
auteurs: Hu Song, Wang Fengjiao, Liu Jia, Zhu Jiaju, Wang Guoyu, Hong Fuxin, He Yulong, Chu Yujie, Kim Daehee
resume: Robot-assisted training (RAT) is widely used in poststroke rehabilitation, but the relationship between training dose and functional recovery remains unclear. This review evaluated the effectiveness of RAT and examined dose-effect relationships. PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and Embase were searched from inception to October 2025. Randomized controlled trials of adults with stroke comparing RAT or RAT combined with conventional rehabilitation (CR) were included. Study quality was assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, and analyses were performed using Review Manager 5.4 and Stata 16.0. Pooled effects were expressed as mean differences (MDs) or standardized MDs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Exploratory subgroup analyses and random-effects meta-regression were conducted across 5 training-dose parameters, and restricted cubic spline analyses assessed nonlinear dose-effect relationships. Evidence certainty was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation. The review was registered with International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251267710). Thirty-six randomized controlled trials involving 1941 patients were included. Compared with CR, RAT significantly improved upper limb motor function (MD = 2.89, 95% CI: 1.49-4.28) and activities of daily living (ADLs; standardized mean difference = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.13-0.43), but not balance function (MD = 1.27, 95% CI: -0.92 to 3.47). Exploratory subgroup analyses showed numerical differences across dose levels, but no between-subgroup differences were significant. None of the 5 training-dose parameters showed significant linear associations with Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity, Berg Balance Scale, or ADL, and restricted cubic spline analyses showed no significant nonlinear associations (all P > .05). Evidence certainty was moderate for Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity and ADL and low for Berg Balance Scale. Dose-related findings should be interpreted cautiously because some subgroups included few studies and actual training dose was incompletely reported. RAT may improve upper limb motor function and ADL after stroke, but has not shown a significant advantage for balance. Current evidence does not demonstrate a clear linear or nonlinear relationship between training dose and rehabilitation outcomes.

titre: Feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of AdaptRehab VR, an immersive virtual reality system for upper limb stroke rehabilitation: A mixed-methods study in Ethiopia.
auteurs: Kenea Chala Diriba, Abessa Teklu Gemechu, Lamba Dheeraj, Bonnechère Bruno
resume: Stroke is a leading cause of long-term disability, with a disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where upper limb impairment emerges as one of its most prevalent and debilitating consequences. Upper limb impairment significantly limits independence and community participation, and this makes rehabilitation a critical priority. While conventional therapy is essential, its effectiveness is often limited by challenges in patient engagement and adherence. To address these barriers, immersive virtual reality (imVR) offers a promising modality for enhancing upper limb rehabilitation. This study examined the feasibility, acceptability, safety, and upper extremity outcomes of the AdaptRehab VR system in Ethiopia with the aim of informing future randomized controlled trials. A mixed-methods design was used, including quantitative assessments of upper extremity function, usability, user experience, and cybersickness, alongside qualitative interviews and focus group discussion (FGD). The study was conducted at Jimma University Teaching Hospital, Ethiopia, and enrolled 20 adults aged ≥18 years with subacute or chronic stroke. Eighteen participants completed nine AdaptRehab VR sessions over three weeks. Physiotherapists collected baseline and post-intervention data. In addition, 18 participants (interview) and 6 physiotherapists (FGD) provided qualitative feedback. The study followed CONSORT guidelines for pilot and feasibility studies. Feasibility was excellent, with 93% adherence. System Usability Scale scores indicated good usability (mean 76.2 ± 12.1). User Experience Questionnaire ratings were positive across attractiveness (1.92 ± 0.84), pragmatic quality (1.78 ± 0.79), and hedonic quality (1.84 ± 0.81). Cybersickness was minimal, with mild transient symptoms (sweating: n = 6; fatigue and headache: n = 3). Significant improvements were observed in the Action Research Arm Test (33.0 ± 13.2 to 48.6 ± 13.1, p < .001), and Box and Block Test (medians of 21.5 to 29, p < .001). Qualitative findings confirmed high acceptability, motivation, and perceived functional gains. The AdaptRehab VR system demonstrated strong feasibility, acceptability, and safety for upper limb stroke rehabilitation in Ethiopia. Positive user experiences and functional improvements support its potential in LMICs settings, warranting a fully powered randomized controlled trial. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07412899.

titre: Functional recovery of patients with moderate and severe traumatic brain injury after extended and standard early rehabilitation.
auteurs: Keleman N, Pilipović N, Sučević Z, Krasnik R, Dragičević-Cvjetković D, Palija S, Bojinović-Rodić D
resume: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is one of the leading causes of morbidity, disability and mortality in all age groups. Treatment and early rehabilitation are crucial to the overall level of recovery. The objective is to compare the effects of standard and extended early rehabilitation on the functional recovery of patients with moderate and severe traumatic brain injury. A prospective experimental study comprised 114 patients with moderate and severe TBI, randomly divided into two groups. The patients of the experimental group had kinesitherapy 7 days a week, twice a day for 45 min, and the patients of the control group had kinesitherapy 7 days a week, twice a day for 30 min. The follow-up parameters were: age sex, clinical characteristics, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), Functional Independence Measure (FIM), Barthel Index (BI) on admission and discharge and Glasgow Outcome Score (GOS) at discharge. 114 patients were randomly divided into two groups of 57 patients each. Males dominate (75.4%), the average age of the sample was Me = 59.0. There was no statistically significant difference between the groups in gender, age and clinical characteristics, GCS on admission; 59(51.8%) patient had severe, 55 (48.2%) moderate TBI, at discharge: 12 (10.5%) had severe, 11(9.6%) moderate and 91(79.8%) mild TBI. FIM of the experimental group was 18 vs. 70 and of the control group was 18 vs. 50, BI of the experimental group was 0 vs. 61 and of the control group was 0 vs. 32. GOS at discharge: complete recovery in the experimental group 9, in the control group 7, mild deficit 22 vs. 15, severe deficit 22 vs. 28, vegetative state 4 vs. 7. Normalized improvement (ratio of achieved progress to maximum possible progress) was higher in the prolonged early rehabilitation group: for FIM (48% vs. 30%), BI (61% vs. 32%) and slightly less for GCS (100% vs. 92%). Although no statistically significant difference on functional recovery between the groups was found, however, a difference in percentage progress was found in favor of extended early rehabilitation, but for a final conclusion it is necessary to make a follow-up after inpatient rehabilitation.

titre: Effects of a Multicomponent Community-Based Intervention Program on Cognitive, Physical, and Psychosocial Outcomes in Older Adults With Mild Cognitive Impairment: An Experimental Study.
auteurs: Tokgöz Gülfidan, Tekin Ebru, Arman Nilay, Irmak Hatice Selin, Katipoğlu Bilal
revue: Journal of aging and physical activity
resume: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in older adults is associated with cognitive decline, reduced independence, and lower quality of life. Early multidimensional interventions may help slow this progression. This study examined the short-term effects of an 8-week Multicomponent Community-Based Intervention Program, integrating physical exercise, creative arts, and psychoeducation on cognitive function, physical performance, and psychosocial well-being in older adults with MCI. A single-group experimental study included 29 older adults diagnosed with MCI. Multi-Community-Based Intervention Program involved weekly or biweekly 5-hr sessions led by a multidisciplinary team of physiotherapists, a gerontologist, a geriatrician, and other experts. The program comprised: (1) exercise workshops (music-based exercise, exergaming, Pilates, Nordic walking, dance therapy, cognitive and exercises); (2) art-based workshops (calligraphy, soap/candle making, and culinary arts); and (3) educational sessions on caregiving, fall prevention, assistive technology, and community resources. Cognitive performance was assessed via Mini-Mental State Examination and Montreal Cognitive Assessment, physical fitness via handgrip strength and flexibility, physical activity via metabolic equivalent scores and calories burned, and psychosocial well-being via CASP-19 and qualitative interviews. Significant improvements were observed in Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores (p = .036), flexibility (p = .021), and physical activity (p < .05). Quality of life scores improved, though not statistically significant. Interviews indicated enhanced emotional satisfaction, social engagement, and motivation to continue activities. Multi-Community-Based Intervention Program is a feasible and beneficial approach for supporting cognitive, physical, and psychosocial health in older adults with MCI. Significance/Implications: Community-based, multidomain interventions integrating physical, cognitive, and psychosocial components may promote functional independence and quality of life, highlighting the potential for scalable preventive strategies in aging populations.

titre: Acceptability of two smart mobility aids: perspectives of healthcare professionals and management working in long term care settings.
auteurs: Best Krista L, Cézé Estelle, Dandois Marie, Piette Patrice, Letoullec Elodie, Lefort Mathilde, Routhier Francois, Leblong Emilie, Fraudet Bastien
resume: Two smart walking aid aids were conceptualised to respond to mobility needs of older adults, including a Walker with Intelligent and Safe Navigation (DENIS), and an Individual Vehicle with Intelligent Verticalization and Navigation Aid for Autonomy (VIVIANA). The aim of this study was to explore perceived acceptability of DENIS and VIVIANA among healthcare professionals (HCPs), specifically exploring factors that influence intention to use. An exploratory multi-method study was conducted. Acceptability of the concepts for DENIS and VIVIANA were explored among HCPs working in LTC settings. HCPs completed the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) questionnaire to explore performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions. Semi-structured individual and group discussions were used to descriptively nuance the same constructs. Correlations and multivariate regression analyses were conducted to explore predictors of intention to use and future use. Individual and group discussions were narratively summarised. Thirty-nine HCPs with 15.3 ± 9.2 years of experience completed the UTAUT and participated in individual or group discussions. HCPs reported high acceptability and intention to use both technologies in the future. Intention to use DENIS was predicted by profession and social influence, while effort expectancy was the main predictor of intention to use VIVIANA. Both smart mobility aids were deemed acceptable by HCPs. Practical considerations such as training, cost, and maintenance highlight the importance of actively involving HCPs in the design and implementation of these technologies in LTC settings.
