titre: Research on the effects of signature size on experts' opinions.
titre_fr: Research on the effects of signature size on experts' opinions.
auteurs: Di̇ncer Mehmet, Canturk Nergis, Dagalp Rukiye, Seyhan Ercan
resume: A signature is writing and/or signs that contain the signatory's personal characteristics and are used to indicate that people accept the authenticity of the formal and private transactions made by themselves in their daily lives and responsibilities arising from those transactions. If the documents are subject to forensic investigation and trial, forensic signature-examination experts are consulted to determine the identity of signatories. The experts reach an opinion at the end of their examinations and comparisons. But some issues affect the process of forming an accurate and reliable expert opinion about a questioned signature. In this study, the aim is to determine whether signatures differ across fields of different sizes and whether these changes affect examiners' opinions. Within the framework of the study, signature samples were collected using a signature form from a total of 60 volunteer participants who declared that they are healthy and who are at least high school graduates, between 19 and 65 years old, who are university and postgraduate students of the Institute of Forensic Sciences of Ankara University. The signatures in the smallest-sized boxes (2 ×0.5 cm) and the signatures on the larger-sized boxes, as well as the guidelines on the signature form, were compared and examined by the researcher according to 16 examination criteria using technical devices in a laboratory environment. In addition to the researcher, three handwriting and document examination experts examined the signatures on the signature forms. The data obtained from the study were analyzed using SPSS 20. The results show that signatures in the smallest areas exhibit significant changes in signature size, whereas criteria such as line quality, pen pressure, curls, and upward movements. Additionally, it was observed that the signature's size also influenced the experts' opinions. The Kruskal-Wallis test was used to assess whether the observed changes in participants' signatures and experts' views were associated with demographic variables, including gender, age group, and dominant hand. It was concluded that the initial movements of the signatures differed significantly according to the gender variable, and the pen pressure criterion differed significantly according to the dominant hand variable. However, no significant differences were observed in other criteria or expert opinions regarding the variables of gender, age group, and dominant hand.

titre: Transdiagnostic Efficacy, Durability, and Optimal Parameters of rTMS for Cognitive Rehabilitation: A Comprehensive Meta-Analysis.
titre_fr: Transdiagnostic Efficacy, Durability, and Optimal Parameters of rTMS for Cognitive Rehabilitation: A Comprehensive Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: Ali Ahmad M S, Gorter Maxine, Zakaria Rasheed, Jenkinson Michael D, Frank Bernhard, Klein Martin, de Witt Hamer Philip C, Douw Linda
resume: Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) is a promising non-invasive neuromodulation technique for cognitive rehabilitation. We evaluated the cognitive effects of rTMS on neurological and psychiatric diseases to determine moderators of efficacy. A meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) comparing real versus sham rTMS to July 2025 was performed. Objective cognition reported as primary or secondary outcomes were extracted and Hedges' g effect sizes computed. Univariate and multivariate three-level meta-analyses were performed to estimate pooled effect sizes and assess moderator influence. 748 measures from 137 studies (5,972 participants) were extracted. Real rTMS produced a significant cognitive enhancement (g=0.28, p<0.0001, I2=37.3%). This was durable over 2-52 weeks follow-up. There was efficacy across all cognitive domains (g>0.20, I2=35.8). Neurodegenerative (g=0.35) and focal (g=0.44) conditions demonstrated stronger effects than psychiatric conditions (g=0.20). Although stimulation target was not a significant moderator overall, the Inferior Frontal Gyrus showed the largest effect (g=0.45), with significant effects also at the left and right DLPFC and left parietal cortex (g=0.29-0.45), all nodes of the Frontoparietal Network. 1-Hz stimulation produced a significantly larger effect (g=0.39) than the 10-Hz reference (g=0.19); 5-Hz, 20-Hz and iTBS were also significantly positive (g=0.30-0.49). In multivariate models, adding 10 rTMS sessions improved cognitive outcomes (Δg=+0.077), whereas increasing the number of pulses per session trended toward reduced efficacy. All effects were confirmed in a left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex subgroup analysis. Subjective cognition was measured in only 6% of studies. A multivariate prediction tool is introduced: https://amsali.shinyapps.io/tms_cognition_prediction/ CONCLUSION: This meta-analysis demonstrates the sustained efficacy of rTMS in enhancing cognitive function, with small-to-moderate effect sizes across diverse clinical populations and stimulation protocols. However, a significant gap remains regarding whether these objective neurocognitive gains translate into meaningful improvements in subjective cognition or functional outcomes.

titre: Effects of visual remediation on contour integration performance in schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
titre_fr: Effects of visual remediation on contour integration performance in schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
auteurs: Kaiser Kaitlyn A, Thompson Judy L, Butler Pamela D, Ahmed Anthony O, Seitz Aaron R, Munneke Jaap, Bell Jewel, Silverstein Steven M
resume: Impairments in visual processing, including difficulties in perceptual organization, are well documented in schizophrenia and related serious mental illnesses. These impairments are thought to contribute to reductions in higher-order cognition and functioning. The present study examined whether a visual remediation intervention targeting low- and mid-level visual processing improves perceptual organization in this population. Participants with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder were randomized to visual remediation (VR) or an active control (AC) condition. The VR intervention targeted contrast sensitivity and contour integration, and perceptual organization was assessed using the Jittered Orientation Visual Integration (JOVI) task. Primary analyses focused on participants who completed the task at baseline, mid-treatment, and post-treatment (N = 50; VR: n = 26; AC: n = 24). Linear mixed-effects models examined JOVI performance as a function of treatment condition, timepoint, and task difficulty (jitter), with planned contrasts testing differential change over time. A significant treatment condition × timepoint interaction indicated that changes in performance differed between groups. Planned difference-in-differences contrasts showed that the VR group exhibited greater improvement from baseline to mid-treatment (estimate = 5.03, p < .001) and from baseline to post-treatment (estimate = 4.30, p = .005) relative to AC. VR targeting low- and mid-level visual processes improved perceptual organization performance relative to an AC condition in participants with a schizophrenia spectrum disorder. These effects emerged early in training and persisted to the post-treatment assessment, supporting the effectiveness of interventions targeting visual processes for improving perceptual organization in this population.

titre: Interventions to reduce cognitive decline post-stroke: an umbrella review.
titre_fr: Interventions to reduce cognitive decline post-stroke: an umbrella review.
auteurs: Tang Eugene Yee Hing, Jackson Emma, Bajpai Ram, Di Bernardo Adriana, Fatima Mishal, Hamza Muhammad, Dunne Jennifer, Grammatikos Paula, Burley Claire V, De Ivey Rhiannon, Mohammed Khalifa, Demeyere Nele, Errington Linda, Stephan Blossom Christa Maree, Robinson Louise, Price Christopher, Quinn Terence
resume: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) remains a common problem that can lead to significant disability and dependency. Previous work suggested that methodologically robust trials were lacking and that there is continued uncertainty on the benefits and limitations of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions. This umbrella review aims to update and synthesise evidence on pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions for PSCI. This review was pre-registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024611909) with searches from 2019 to 2024. Eligible studies were systematic reviews (SRs) of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating pharmacological or non-pharmacological interventions in adult stroke survivors (≥18 years) of any severity and reporting change in global cognition (eg, Mini-Mental State Examination). AMSTAR2 was used for risk of bias. Of 4889 records identified, 69 SRs (global cognition data from 747 unique RCTs; 57,176 participants) met inclusion criteria. Interventions were grouped into 37 categories including both single (eg, acupuncture, exercise, cognitive rehabilitation) and combined modalities and assessed at categorical level. Most intervention types were associated with statistically significant improvements in global cognition. Substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals indicate that effect sizes may vary considerably across populations and settings. This review identifies promising evidence that several interventions may produce clinically meaningful improvements in global cognition post-stroke. However, confidence in this evidence is low: despite a substantial increase in the number of RCTs most included reviews were rated as critically low in quality with methodological limitations. Current evidence is insufficient to support firm recommendations for the inclusion of specific interventions in guidance.

titre: Persistent Choice reaction-time slowing in collegiate athletes with a history of concussion.
titre_fr: Persistent Choice reaction-time slowing in collegiate athletes with a history of concussion.
auteurs: Mohammadi Amin, Lawton Joshua T, Schussler Eric, Campbell Thomas R
resume: To determine whether collegiate athletes with a history of concussion exhibit persistent reaction-time deficits after accounting for SCAT6-based memory/concentration measures and computerized neurocognitive domain scores. 547 NCAA Division I athletes completed computerized neurocognitive testing, SCAT6-based symptom and cognitive assessments, and balance evaluations. Propensity-score matching produced 138 athletes with concussion history matched to 138 controls. Four RT outcomes were analyzed: Choice RT, Simple RT, Stroop RT, and Shifting-Attention RT. Multivariate analyses of covariance (MANCOVA) examined group differences controlling for SCAT6-based memory and concentration measures and CNS Vital Signs cognitive domain scores. Athletes with a prior concussion demonstrated significantly slower Choice RT both before adjustment (p = 0.019) and after controlling for all covariates (p = 0.006). No significant group differences emerged for Simple RT, Stroop RT, or Shifting-Attention RT (all p 0 > .53). Executive function, cognitive flexibility, and visual memory showed consistent associations with RT performance across outcomes. History of concussion is selectively associated with persistent slowing in Choice RT, independent of SCAT6-based memory and concentration measures and CNS Vital Signs cognitive domain scores. Choice RT may be a sensitive marker of subtle neurocognitive slowing and may help inform both post-concussion assessment and rehabilitation planning.

titre: Virtual and Augmented Reality for Cognitive and Language Rehabilitation in Children and Adolescents: A Scoping Review.
titre_fr: Virtual and Augmented Reality for Cognitive and Language Rehabilitation in Children and Adolescents: A Scoping Review.
auteurs: Pagano Maria, Cappadona Irene, Anselmo Anna, Codispoto Alessio, Cardile Davide, De Luca Rosaria, Quartarone Angelo, Calabrò Rocco Salvatore, Corallo Francesco
resume: Background: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used in pediatric rehabilitation to deliver engaging, adaptive, and ecologically relevant interventions. Objective: To map the available evidence on VR interventions targeting cognitive and linguistic functions in pediatric populations, focusing on intervention characteristics, technologies, outcome domains. Methods: A scoping review was conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, IEEE Xplore, Embase, PsycINFO and Scopus without publication-date restrictions. English-language journal articles involving participants younger than 18 years were considered. Eligible interventions targeted attention, executive functions, memory, processing speed, language, speech, or related cognitive-linguistic abilities. Methodological quality was assessed using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklists. Results: Twelve studies were included. Considerable heterogeneity was observed in populations, treatment intensity, comparator conditions, technologies, and outcome measures. The most consistent benefits concerned attention and executive functions, particularly inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory, planning, processing speed, and metacognition. Evidence for language, memory, and social cognition was promising but more limited. Positive findings were reported across immersive, semi-immersive, and non-immersive VR systems, with no clear evidence of superiority according to level of immersion. Follow-up assessments were uncommon, and methodological quality was heterogeneous across study designs. Conclusions: VR interventions appear promising for pediatric cognitive and language rehabilitation. resume_fr: Background: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used in pediatric rehabilitation to deliver engaging, adaptive, and ecologically relevant interventions. Objective: To map the available evidence on VR interventions targeting cognitive and linguistic functions in pediatric populations, focusing on intervention characteristics, technologies, outcome domains. Methods: A scoping review was conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, IEEE Xplore, Embase, PsycINFO and Scopus without publication-date restrictions. English-language journal articles involving participants younger than 18 years were considered. Eligible interventions targeted attention, executive functions, memory, processing speed, language, speech, or related cognitive-linguistic abilities. Methodological quality was assessed using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklists. Results: Twelve studies were included. Considerable heterogeneity was observed in populations, treatment intensity, comparator conditions, technologies, and outcome measures. The most consistent benefits concerned attention and executive functions, particularly inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory, planning, processing speed, and metacognition. Evidence for language, memory, and social cognition was promising but more limited. Positive findings were reported across immersive, semi-immersive, and non-immersive VR systems, with no clear evidence of superiority according to level of immersion. Follow-up assessments were uncommon, and methodological quality was heterogeneous across study designs. Conclusions: VR interventions appear promising for pediatric cognitive and language rehabilitation. Larger controlled studies using standardized outcomes, active comparators, and longer follow-up are needed.

titre: Development of Enhanced Reviews of Psychological Changes After Stroke (ENRICH): A complex Intervention to Monitor and Support Self-Management of Post-Stroke Psychological Changes Within a Matched Care Model.
titre_fr: Development of Enhanced Reviews of Psychological Changes After Stroke (ENRICH): A complex Intervention to Monitor and Support Self-Management of Post-Stroke Psychological Changes Within a Matched Care Model.
auteurs: Hobden Georgina, Demeyere Nele
resume: ObjectiveTo report the design and development of a complex intervention to monitor and support self-management of post-stroke psychological changes.DesignThe Medical Research Council framework for complex intervention research guided development work, which included a literature review, semi-structured interviews with stroke survivors (n = 26) and family members (n = 11), a Delphi survey with healthcare professionals and researchers (n = 42), and workshops with stroke survivors (n = 4), family members (n = 3), and healthcare professionals (n = 5).SettingStroke community care.ParticipantsStroke survivors, family members, healthcare professionals and researchers.InterventionThe Enhanced Reviews of Psychological Changes after stroke (ENRICH) programme is a brief intervention deliverable within the UK matched care model of post-stroke psychological support. It supports stroke survivors with mild to moderate cognitive changes, low mood, anxiety and fatigue by monitoring symptoms, providing personalised psychoeducation, and supporting self-management through three brief reviews at 1, 3, and 6 months. Those with more severe or persistent psychological changes are referred through local care pathways for specialist psychological input.Main measuresThe intervention is reported using the TIDieR checklist.ResultsThe logic model and programme theory suggest benefits for psychological wellbeing and quality of life, with stakeholder input likely to enhance acceptability and feasibility.ConclusionsENRICH has the potential to address gaps in UK post-stroke care for those with mild to moderate changes affecting cognition, mood, anxiety and fatigue when delivered within the matched care model. Feasibility testing is underway with future clinical effectiveness testing is planned.

titre: How inpatients spend their day: A behavioural mapping study of physical, cognitive and social participation across acute and rehabilitation wards.
titre_fr: How inpatients spend their day: A behavioural mapping study of physical, cognitive and social participation across acute and rehabilitation wards.
auteurs: Barrett Stephen, Procter Jacob, Sun Wonbin, Dunford Ashley R, McCrae Prue, Maher Carol, Mudge Alison
resume: ObjectiveTo describe and compare patterns of physical, cognitive and social activity across inpatient wards in a regional hospital.DesignProspective observational study using behavioural mapping.SettingFive inpatient wards (three acute, two rehabilitation) in a regional public hospital in Australia.ParticipantsA total of 151 inpatients were observed over five weekdays between March and April 2025.Main measuresBehavioural mapping was conducted from 08:00 to 16:00 using a standardised protocol. At each observation, four domains were recorded: location, body position, activity and social context (presence of others). Proportions within each category were summarised descriptively for each ward.ResultsAcross 6804 data points recorded, patients spent most of their observed time in their bedrooms (85-100% across wards). In acute wards, patients were predominantly on or in bed (65%-100%); rehabilitation wards demonstrated lower but still substantial time on or in bed (37%-45%). Walking or standing accounted for ≤13% of body-position observations, and structured exercise was infrequent (0%-14% of activity observations). Patients were alone for 50%-67% of observations. Differences between acute and rehabilitation wards were modest, with rehabilitation wards demonstrating greater sitting out of bed but similarly low upright mobility.ConclusionsAcross acute and rehabilitation settings, patients spent most of the daytime hours in bed and alone, with limited physical activity. The consistency of these behaviours across wards suggests inactivity and isolation reflect routine hospital environments rather than individual patient motivation. System-level strategies that reshape hospital routines and environments may be required to meaningfully increase participation during admission.

titre: Effects of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation on global cognitive performance and activities of daily living in post-stroke patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
titre_fr: Effects of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation on global cognitive performance and activities of daily living in post-stroke patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
auteurs: Wang Mingchen, Wang Guan
resume: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) severely affects patients' daily living and independence, with limited treatment options. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) shows promise but inconsistencies in reported effect sizes across cognitive domains. We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and EMBASE up to March 2026 for randomized controlled trials evaluating rTMS combined with rehabilitation versus sham or rehabilitation alone in stroke patients. Outcomes included MMSE, MoCA, Digit Span Test (DST), and modified Barthel Index (MBI). Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4. Ten RCTs involving 666 patients were included. rTMS significantly improved MMSE (MD = 1.76, 95%CI[1.10, 2.43], p < 0.00001, I2 = 5%) and MoCA scores (MD = 2.64, 95% CI[1.74,3.55], p < 0.00001, I2 = 0%). No significant effect was found on DST-forward (p = 0.13), but DST-backward showed mild improvement (MD = 0.77, 95% CI[0.35,1.18], p = 0.0003, I2 = 62%). MBI scores were significantly enhanced (MD = 10.68, 95% CI[7.91,13.46], p < 0.00001, I2 = 0%). Based on low-to-moderate certainty evidence, rTMS combined with rehabilitation may improve global cognitive screening performance and daily living ability in stroke patients, with a mild benefit on working memory. Further studies are needed to optimize stimulation protocols.

titre: Joint-brain communication in rheumatoid arthritis: glial mechanisms, pain phenotypes, and translational evidence.
titre_fr: Joint-brain communication in rheumatoid arthritis: glial mechanisms, pain phenotypes, and translational evidence.
auteurs: Guo Dong, Xu Ke, Xiao Lin, Li Hui, Li Zheng, Pan Ying, Zhang Huan
resume: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease in which persistent pain, fatigue, cognitive impairment, depression, and anxiety may involve altered central nervous system (CNS) processing. This narrative review synthesizes preclinical and clinical evidence concerning proposed glial cell-mediated joint-brain communication in RA. Joint-derived neural inputs and systemic inflammatory signals may communicate with the CNS through humoral, cellular, neural, neuroendocrine, and neurovascular pathways. Preclinical studies implicate microglia and astrocytes in neuroinflammatory responses, spinal central sensitization, impaired hippocampal plasticity, and neurovascular alterations. Human studies associate systemic inflammation with altered brain connectivity and CNS-related symptoms. Disease-modifying antirheumatic treatment, particularly tumor necrosis factor inhibition, has been associated with improvements in selected CNS-related outcomes. Adjunctive symptom management includes phenotype-guided analgesic approaches, rehabilitation, and psychological and sleep-focused interventions. Translational research explores glial modulators, pathway-specific interventions, vagal neuromodulation, neuroimaging, cerebrospinal fluid markers, and multidimensional patient stratification. The proposed joint-brain framework highlights the value of assessing inflammation alongside pain phenotype, cognition, mood, fatigue, sleep, and function. Future human studies should evaluate whether mechanistic and biomarker findings can improve individualized treatment selection and clinical outcomes.

titre: Validation of the comprehensive ICF Core Set for burn injury rehabilitation from the perspective of occupational therapists and patients.
titre_fr: Validation of the comprehensive ICF Core Set for burn injury rehabilitation from the perspective of occupational therapists and patients.
auteurs: Hamedi Dorsa, Hassani Mehraban Afsoon, Dahmardehei Mostafa, Abolghasemi Jamileh, Lajevardi Laleh
resume: This study aimed to validate the ICF-CS for burn injury rehabilitation from the perspective of occupational therapists (OTs) and patients. A two-round Delphi study was held with experienced OTs specializing in burn rehabilitation who were also familiar with the ICF framework. These experts contributed through a hybrid panel. Codes were retained if they achieved a consensus threshold of ≥75%. Patient perspectives were collected through semi-structured individual interviews, and their suggestions were subsequently linked to ICF codes. Fourteen OTs and nineteen patients participated in this study. Of the 68 original codes, more than 80% reached consensus endorsement. Based on experts' input, 17 new codes were incorporated into the ICF-CS: one in the body functions, ten in the activities and participation (AP), and six in the environmental factors. Additionally, eight new codes were derived from patient input-four related to AP and four linked to environmental factors-which overlapped with experts' suggestions. The ICF-CS for burn injury rehabilitation received strong endorsement from OTs and patients. The greater emphasis on the AP domain reflects the central role of occupational therapy in healthcare. Furthermore, environmental factors-shaped by national policies and sociocultural contexts-require greater attention in localized adaptations.

titre: Anatomy, aetiology, clinical presentation, classification, diagnosis, and non-surgical management of triangular fibrocartilage complex tears: a narrative review.
titre_fr: Anatomy, aetiology, clinical presentation, classification, diagnosis, and non-surgical management of triangular fibrocartilage complex tears: a narrative review.
auteurs: Liu Peng, Zhou Tianyu
revue: Frontiers in sports and active living
resume: Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) injuries are a common source of ulnar-sided wrist pain and functional impairment, particularly in athletes and individuals engaged in upper-limb-dominant or wrist-loading activities. Despite their prevalence, standardised, non-surgical treatment pathways remain underdeveloped. This narrative review aims to critically synthesise and discuss current evidence on the non-surgical management of TFCC injuries in physically active adults. Narrative review. A structured literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for English-language studies published from January 2015 to May 2025. The identified studies focusing on the non-surgical management of TFCC injuries were screened and included. Current evidence suggests a range of non-surgical interventions for pain reduction and functional improvement in TFCC injuries across different clinical presentations, including rest, splinting, physical therapy, NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections, and progressive functional rehabilitation. Adjunctive modalities such as extracorporeal shock wave therapy and platelet-rich plasma injections also show potential benefits. However, important gaps persist in TFCC classification-specific treatment recommendations, the standardisation of rehabilitation protocols, and the integration of emerging therapies. This review synthesises current evidence on the non-surgical management of TFCC injuries. Recognising differences in injury mechanism, particularly between acute trauma-related and repetitive overuse-related degenerative presentations, it proposes a structured, phase-based rehabilitation framework for TFCC lesions with an intact distal radioulnar joint. The framework emphasises presentation-specific early management, progressive tissue loading, and functional reintegration. This review provides clinicians with a conceptual, non-surgical framework to guide the management of TFCC injuries, aiming to support pain reduction and functional recovery in physically active adults. While surgical options for TFCC injuries are well established, standardised non-surgical pathways remain underdeveloped and diagnosis can be challenging due to overlapping presentations. This review summarises current evidence on non-surgical TFCC management, including conventional and emerging therapies, and outlines a stage-based approach derived from available literature and clinical reasoning to support individualised non-surgical care.

titre: Do patients give a damn? An exploratory study of patient perspectives on clinician swearing during physical rehabilitation.
titre_fr: Do patients give a damn? An exploratory study of patient perspectives on clinician swearing during physical rehabilitation.
auteurs: Mercer Andrew, Meakins Adam, St Martin Roxanne, Trummer Garrett, Geoghagan Libbi, Muscha Kara, Washmuth Nicholas B
resume: Swearing is a common linguistic tool associated with positive benefits. In healthcare, however, the impact of clinician swearing on patients remains unclear. This exploratory study investigated patients' lived experiences with clinicians who swore and examined patient perspectives on when clinician swearing is perceived as appropriate or inappropriate. A cross-sectional, mixed methods, retrospective study was conducted with physical rehabilitation patients (N = 57). Patients completed an ad hoc survey assessing experiences, perceptions, and attitudes toward clinician swearing. Logistic regressions tested whether clinician swearing frequency predicted the following patient reported outcomes: motivation, self-confidence, and treatment adherence. Linear regressions evaluated whether clinician swearing frequency predicted: professionalism, patient-centeredness, offensiveness, and ability to enhance the rehabilitation experience. Qualitative responses were analyzed using cognitive network analyses. Thirty-one patients (54.39%) reported that their clinician swore during treatment. Among these, most indicated swearing increased motivation (61.13%), improved self-confidence (58.06%), and supported adherence (51.61%). Patients generally agreed that swearing was patient-centered (54.84%) and improved the rehabilitation experience (64.52%), while no patients stated the swearing was unprofessional or offensive. When swearing frequency was dichotomized into high vs. low, patients in the high-frequency group reported greater motivation, self-confidence, and adherence compared to the low-frequency group, though confidence intervals included null effects. However, the small sample size limited statistical power; therefore, these nonsignificant findings should be interpreted cautiously. High-frequency swearing was associated with higher ratings of patient centeredness [B = -1.00, 95% CI (-1.95, -0.05), p = 0.04]. Qualitative findings indicated swearing was considered appropriate when used to build rapport, comfort, or motivate, and inappropriate with young or older patients, when directed at rather than with patients, or during serious discussions. Due to the study's limitations, the findings should be interpreted with caution. Most patients who experienced clinician swearing reported neutral to positive outcomes, suggesting swearing may enhance aspects of rehabilitation. Patients emphasized that appropriateness depends on context, relationship, and patient characteristics, suggesting that swearing may be a potentially effective communicative tool best applied with sensitivity.

titre: Impact of Virtual Reality Training on Quality of Life, Diaphragmatic Excursion, Pulmonary Function, and Respiratory Muscle Strength After Upper Abdominal Surgeries: A Randomized Controlled Study.
titre_fr: Impact of Virtual Reality Training on Quality of Life, Diaphragmatic Excursion, Pulmonary Function, and Respiratory Muscle Strength After Upper Abdominal Surgeries: A Randomized Controlled Study.
auteurs: Allam Nesma M, Abdel-Aal Nabil Mahmoud, Abd El-Azeim Alshaymaa S, Eladl Hadaya Mosaad
resume: Adding virtual reality exercise (VRE) to conventional physical therapy (CPT) may reduce upper abdominal surgery complications. The objective of the study was to evaluate the effects of VRE on quality of life (QoL), diaphragmatic excursion, pulmonary function, respiratory muscle strength, and functional capacity after upper abdominal surgeries. This was a randomized controlled trial. The setting was a physical therapy outpatient clinic. Participants were 120 patients (20-65 years old) with upper abdominal surgeries. They were randomly assigned to a VRE group or a control group. The VRE group received 5 interactive games plus CPT; the control group received CPT alone, with supervised sessions 5 times weekly for 8 weeks. The primary outcome was QoL. Secondary outcomes included diaphragmatic excursion, forced vital capacity, forced expiratory volume in 1 second, peak expiratory flow, maximum inspiratory and expiratory pressures, and functional capacity, measured at baseline and after intervention. Following trial registration and prior to data analysis, the primary outcome was revised from pulmonary function to QoL to better reflect the multidimensional objectives of the intervention; all originally registered outcomes were retained and reported as secondary outcomes. After intervention, the results revealed statistically significant differences between groups in QoL domains, with more favor to the VRE group. Mean differences and 95% CIs between the groups were 20.28 (95% CI = 18.09 to 22.48) for physical health, 23.8 (95% CI = 21.9 to 25.7) for psychological health, 22.98 (95% CI = 20.92 to 25.05) for social relationships, and 21.77 (95% CI = 19.8 to 23.73) for environmental health. Integrating VRE with CPT produced clinically meaningful short-term improvements in QoL, pulmonary function, respiratory muscle strength, diaphragmatic excursion, and functional capacity compared with CPT alone following upper abdominal surgery. These findings support the use of VRE as an effective adjunct to postoperative rehabilitation. However, the results should be interpreted with caution due to the short follow-up period and the inability to blind participants to group allocation.

titre: Therapeutic alliance development in physical therapy for people with serious mental illness: a qualitative study.
titre_fr: Therapeutic alliance development in physical therapy for people with serious mental illness: a qualitative study.
auteurs: Cimmino Meredith, Zechner Michelle, Fluet Gerard, Rothpletz-Puglia Pamela, Nonoyama Saren
resume: Physical therapy (PT) has been demonstrated to be beneficial for people with serious mental illness (SMI). Literature in this field is emerging and growing rapidly. However, little is known about how therapeutic relationships are formed in PT for people with SMI. Expanding our knowledge of how people with serious mental illness perceive and experience their relationships with physical therapists, and how these perceptions impact the development of therapeutic alliance (TA), may inform the development of strategies to enhance TA. The purpose of this study was to explore how people with SMI perceive the development of TA with their therapists during PT. This study employed an interpretive descriptive qualitative approach, utilizing interviews with study participants. This qualitative study analyzed interview transcripts from 30 adults with SMI who had received skilled PT. Interview transcripts were analyzed using inductive and deductive applied thematic analysis, informed by Peplau's Interpersonal Relations Theory and core principles of psychiatric rehabilitation. Six themes were generated: 1) orient to care, 2) develop a strong relationship, 3) provide person-centered care, 4) importance of life history, 5) it takes time, and 6) empower to get better. The findings of this study provide preliminary evidence supporting factors that drive the development of a therapeutic alliance for individuals with SMI in PT. Our findings suggest that PTs treating people with SMI should consider: 1) offering a pre-examination orientation using Peplau's Interpersonal Relations Theory as a guide; 2) allow for extra time for relationship building; 3) engage clients as active partners throughout the rehabilitation process; and 4) demonstrate respect for a patient with SMI's personal boundaries during all stages of care. These recommendations are supported by the core psychiatric rehabilitation principles of empowerment, person-centered care, and collaborative partnership. Adding them to PT practice may enhance engagement in rehabilitation for people with SMI, making PT more inclusive and recovery-oriented.

Six themes were generated: 1) orient to care, 2) develop a strong relationship, 3) provide person-centered care, 4) importance of life history, 5) it takes time, and 6) empower to get better. The findings of this study provide preliminary evidence supporting factors that drive the development of a therapeutic alliance for individuals with SMI in PT. Our findings suggest that PTs treating people with SMI should consider: 1) offering a pre-examination orientation using Peplau's Interpersonal Relations Theory as a guide; 2) allow for extra time for relationship building; 3) engage clients as active partners throughout the rehabilitation process; and 4) demonstrate respect for a patient with SMI's personal boundaries during all stages of care. These recommendations are supported by the core psychiatric rehabilitation principles of empowerment, person-centered care, and collaborative partnership. Adding them to PT practice may enhance engagement in rehabilitation for people with SMI, making PT more inclusive and recovery-oriented.

titre: Additional Effects of Manual Therapy to Exercise on Pain and Function in Individuals With Knee Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
titre_fr: Additional Effects of Manual Therapy to Exercise on Pain and Function in Individuals With Knee Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: da Silva Viviane R, Ramalho Rebecca B, de Noronha Marcos, Bracht Marcelo A, Tavares Luiz Felipe, Selistre Luiz F A
resume: This systematic review aimed to analyse the additional effects of manual therapy (MT) to exercise (EX) compared to EX alone on pain, function, and PPT in individuals with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Six databases (MEDLINE, PEDro, EMBASE, CENTRAL, CINAHL, and Web of Science) were searched from inception up to May 2026. Two independent reviewers selected randomized clinical trials. Standardized mean differences (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated by random-effects for meta-analyses. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024525169), and the certainty of a body of evidence was classified using GRADE. Twenty-nine studies were included. MT combined with EX, compared to EX alone, reduced pain in the immediate (mean difference [MD] = -0.53; 95% CI = -0.97 to -0.09 very low certainty of evidence), short-term (MD = -1.30; 95% CI = -1.74 to -0.87 very low certainty of evidence), and medium-term (MD = -0.98; 95% CI = -1.86 to -0.10 moderate certainty of evidence). Function also improved in the short-term (SMD = -0.89; 95% CI = -1.49 to -0.29 very low certainty of evidence) and medium-term (SMD = -0.62; 95% CI = -1.13 to -0.10 very low certainty of evidence). However, no significant long-term effects were observed for either pain and function. No eligible studies assessing pressure pain threshold (PPT) were identified. An additional effect of MT to EX was observed; however, the certainty of the evidence was very low to low. MT can be considered an adjunctive intervention in KOA, as it appears to provide short-duration effects on both pain relief and functional outcomes, but does not seem to extend to the long term. This systematic review identifies that MT can be considered a complementary intervention when combined with EX, which appears to provide immediate, short- and medium-term effects, both in pain relief and functional outcomes in KOA. The use of MT with EX may assist patients at the beginning of the rehabilitation process. However, its benefits do not appear to extend to the long term, highlighting that MT can serve as a strategy to support exercise, particularly during the initial phase of treatment.

titre: Percussive Vibration Therapy as an Adjunct to Conventional Physiotherapy in Chronic Non-Specific Low Back Pain: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
titre_fr: Percussive Vibration Therapy as an Adjunct to Conventional Physiotherapy in Chronic Non-Specific Low Back Pain: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
auteurs: Bayraktar Elif Esma, Şevgin Ömer, Vahedi Ainaz, Safran Ertuğrul
resume: Background/Objectives: Hand-held percussive vibration therapy (PVT) is widely used in musculoskeletal rehabilitation, yet its incremental benefit beyond an active physiotherapy program for chronic non-specific low back pain (CNLBP) is unclear. We investigated whether PVT added to conventional physiotherapy (CPT) improves disability, sleep quality, and pain. Methods: This single-center, parallel-group, assessor-blinded randomized trial enrolled 50 adults aged 18-65 years with CNLBP and baseline visual analogue scale (VAS) pain ≥4/10. Participants were allocated equally to PVT + CPT or CPT alone and attended three sessions weekly for eight weeks. The Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) was the primary outcome; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and VAS scores were secondary outcomes. Week-8 scores were analyzed with baseline-adjusted ANCOVA using HC3 robust standard errors. Results: Follow-up data were complete for all participants. The adjusted ODI score at week 8 was 2.59 points higher with PVT + CPT than with CPT (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.47 to 4.71; p = 0.017), a statistically significant difference in favor of CPT. PSQI scores did not differ between groups (adjusted difference, 0.25; 95% CI, -0.40 to 0.90; p = 0.451). VAS scores were lower with PVT + CPT (adjusted difference, -1.15; 95% CI, -1.45 to -0.85; p < 0.001). Conclusions: PVT did not provide an additional benefit for disability and did not improve sleep quality when added to CPT. The pain difference was a secondary, exploratory finding of uncertain clinical relevance.

titre: Patients' Perspectives on Bedside Manners in Physical Therapy in Saudi Arabia: A Mixed-Methods Study.
titre_fr: Patients' Perspectives on Bedside Manners in Physical Therapy in Saudi Arabia: A Mixed-Methods Study.
auteurs: Aloraini Saleh M, Aba-Alkhayl Faris M, Althinayyan Sara H, Alfouzan Moodhi M, Almohaimeed Fayzah A, Alsughayyir Alanoud I, Aljutaily Raghad, Alquraishi Ruba S, Aldughaim Renad K, Alnoshan Ryhana M, Albarrak Jana B, Alsaheel Wasan A, Alqazlan Fai A, Alsouhibani Ali
resume: Background/Objectives: Bedside manners are central to patient-centered rehabilitation, yet patient perspectives on physical therapy in Saudi Arabia remain underexplored. This study examined patients' perceptions of physical therapists' bedside manners and explored variation according to patient and therapist characteristics. Methods: A cross-sectional convergent mixed-methods study included 510 patients who had completed physical therapy within the previous year. Participants completed a 25-item questionnaire comprising six sociodemographic and 19 bedside-manner items; 25 participants also completed semi-structured interviews. Quantitative data were summarized descriptively, and selected Likert-scale items with sufficient response variability were examined using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests with Bonferroni correction and Cramér's V. Interview data underwent thematic analysis. Results: Responses to the nine yes/no items were predominantly affirmative (88.6-98.6%). The first item assessed familiarity with the term "bedside manners," whereas the remaining eight items assessed patients' reported experiences of therapist behaviors. Agreement exceeded 90% for six of the ten Likert-scale items, while responses regarding empathy, therapist presence, and attention according to case complexity were more variable. After correction for multiple comparisons, preferences regarding therapist presence differed by therapist sex and patient-therapist sex match (both p < 0.001; Cramér's V = 0.17). The qualitative analysis identified seven themes: therapeutic relationship, treatment adherence, nonverbal communication, emotional support, therapist supervision, initial impression, and professional consultation. Conclusions: Patients in this sample strongly valued communication, consent, privacy, reassurance, and respectful interpersonal behavior, while preferences regarding empathy and therapist supervision were more individualized. Interpretation is limited by the cross-sectional convenience sample, restriction to treatment completers, and the small magnitude of the observed associations.

titre: AI-Enabled Telerehabilitation for Chronic Nonspecific Neck Pain: Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.
titre_fr: AI-Enabled Telerehabilitation for Chronic Nonspecific Neck Pain: Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.
auteurs: Zhao Yiwei, Zhang Yanbin, Lin Ye, Liu Di, Zheng Jiamin, Cai Siyi
resume: Exercise therapy is effective in managing chronic nonspecific neck pain (CNP). Nevertheless, the high burden of CNP continues to place pressure on existing rehabilitation services, especially in remote or resource-constrained settings where continuous and standardized physical therapy may be difficult to access. By combining home-based exercise with remote supervision and movement feedback, AI-enabled telerehabilitation may broaden access to rehabilitation and support the continued management of CNP. This study examined whether an AI-enabled telerehabilitation program was noninferior to standard outpatient rehabilitation for improving neck-related disability in individuals with CNP and compared the effects of the 2 interventions on pain, health-related quality of life, and cervical range of motion. This multicenter, prospective, parallel-group randomized noninferiority trial was conducted at Peking Union Medical College Hospital and Beijing Jishuitan Hospital. Patients with CNP of at least 3 months' duration were randomized 1:1 to a telerehabilitation group (TG) or outpatient rehabilitation group (OG) using concealed, web-based, variable blocks stratified by center and baseline Neck Disability Index (NDI) severity. Both groups completed identical 24-week strengthening and stretching programs (3 sessions per wk; ≈30 min per session) and were assessed at weeks 0, 4, 8, 12, and 24. TG trained at home using sensor-based movement recognition and threshold rules; OG received face-to-face outpatient rehabilitation. Week-24 NDI was the primary outcome; Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS), EQ-5D, and cervical range of motion were secondary. Noninferiority required the upper 95% CI bound of the TG-OG NDI difference to be <10 percentage points (5/50). Analyses were intention-to-treat; assessors and statisticians were blinded. Of 312 individuals screened, 116 were randomized (58 per group). At week 24, 55 TG and 53 OG participants completed assessments; all 116 participants were included in the primary intention-to-treat analysis using observed or imputed data. The between-group differences in NDI (TG - OG) were -2.8 (95% CI -6.3 to 0.7; P=.11) at week 12 and -2.5 (95% CI -6.2 to 1.2; P=.15) at week 24. At week 24, the upper 95% CI bound was below the prespecified noninferiority margin of 10 percentage points on the 0 to 100 NDI scale, equivalent to 5 points on the original 0 to 50 scale, demonstrating noninferiority of TG. Both groups showed clinically meaningful reductions in NDI, with comparable improvements in NPRS, EQ-5D, and cervical range of motion. No intervention-related harms occurred. Over 24 weeks, AI-enabled telerehabilitation was noninferior to exercise-matched outpatient rehabilitation for neck-related disability, with broadly comparable improvements in pain, health-related quality of life, and cervical range of motion. AI-enabled telerehabilitation may be a practical alternative for patients with CNP who are unable to attend outpatient rehabilitation.

titre: Persistent Shoulder Instability and Retained Primitive Reflexes. Addressing a Potential Gap in Adult Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation Care.
titre_fr: Persistent Shoulder Instability and Retained Primitive Reflexes. Addressing a Potential Gap in Adult Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation Care.
auteurs: Richardson Ellie, Acharya Ramni, Goodwin Peter C, Lewis Jeremy
resume: SYNOPSIS: Using a case of recalcitrant type III shoulder instability, this editorial explores the potentially overlooked link between retained primitive reflexes and persistent musculoskeletal conditions. We explore how incomplete primitive reflex integration may disrupt motor control, compromise dynamic stability, and interact with neurodevelopmental traits like generalized joint hypermobility. Addressing a potential gap in adult musculoskeletal care, we establish a theoretical framework and foundational justification for future research. To investigate this potential paradigm shift, we outline a 4-stage research road map: mapping existing literature on adult primitive reflexes, validating specific primitive reflex assessment tools in musculoskeletal populations, testing targeted therapeutic integration exercises, and exploring bidirectional symptom relationships. Ultimately, this editorial outlines a clear path forward for decoding neurodevelopmental profiles when traditional physical therapy stalls.

titre: Neuromuscular Electric Stimulation Improves Early Isometric Knee Strength After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction and Repair: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
titre_fr: Neuromuscular Electric Stimulation Improves Early Isometric Knee Strength After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction and Repair: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
auteurs: Daud Anser, Lameire Darius Luke, Schemitsch Geoffrey William, Whelan Daniel Burke, Dwyer Tim, Theodoropoulos John, Chahal Jaskarndip
revue: Arthroscopy : the journal of arthroscopic & related surgery : official publication of the Arthroscopy Association of North America and the International Arthroscopy Association
resume: To assess the effectiveness of neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) on quadriceps strength and knee function after anterior cruciate ligament surgery. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE, and Embase from inception until February 2025 was conducted. Randomized controlled trials on adults undergoing anterior cruciate ligament surgery with NMES as an intervention and standard rehabilitation as a control were included. Study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool were performed independently by 2 reviewers. Meta-analysis including subgroup and heterogeneity analysis was conducted using Cochrane RevMan 10.0.1. Twenty-one randomized controlled trial studies met our inclusion criteria (n = 687 patients, 314 control and 373 NMES patients). The frequency-weighted mean age of included patients across all studies was 27.0 years. Mean follow-up time was 18.4 weeks (4-54). Pooled analysis for isometric knee extension strength showed statistically significant improvements in absolute strength between NMES (n = 54 patients) and control (n = 55 patients) groups (n = 109 patients, mean difference 0.24; 95% confidence interval 0.2-0.27; P < .01, I<sup>2</sup> = 9%) and strength as a percentage of the uninvolved limb between NMES (n = 131) and control (n = 133 patients) groups (n = 264 patients, standardized mean difference 0.87; 95% confidence interval 0.11-1.64; P = .03, I<sup>2</sup> = 87%) in the early (6-12 weeks) but not late postoperative period (>12 weeks). Similar statistical significance was noted with improvements in knee flexion (P = .01), thigh circumference (P = .04), and Lysholm scores (P = .02) but not International Knee Documentation Committee scores. Four studies reporting isokinetic muscle strength were pooled, and no statistically significant difference was found. The use of NMES as an adjunct to a standard physical therapy program after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction appears to modestly improve isometric strength at a faster rate than standard rehabilitation alone. No conclusion can be made regarding the functional recovery or improvements in knee strength beyond the 3-month postoperative period. Level I, meta-analysis of randomized controlled trial studies.

titre: Research priorities to advance the physiotherapy profession: a concept-mapping study informed by the global physiotherapy community.
titre_fr: Research priorities to advance the physiotherapy profession: a concept-mapping study informed by the global physiotherapy community.
auteurs: Whittaker Jackie L, Donaldson Alex, Kosakowski Heidi, Alvis Karim, Deutsch Judith E, Elkins Mark R, Feys Peter, Mudzi Witness, Sharma Saurab, Mueller-Winkler Birgit
resume: What research areas need to be addressed to advance the physiotherapy profession globally? Mixed methods. Seventy-four individuals with advanced physiotherapy profession knowledge contributed to a five-step participatory concept-mapping process. Participants brainstormed statements in response to the above question (n = 49) and then thematically sorted (n = 29) and rated (n = 31) them for importance and feasibility (5-point Likert scales). Statements were grouped using multidimensional scaling and hierarchical cluster analyses, and the final cluster solution and conceptual fit of statements were iteratively reviewed and refined to optimise conceptual congruence. Sixty-four unique statements were brainstormed, sorted and rated. A nine-cluster map was identified as the most appropriate representation of the data. From most to least important (number of statements, cluster mean importance/5), the clusters were: 'Prevention and rehabilitation across the lifespan' (7, 3.59); 'Technology, innovation and digital transformation' (6, 3.45); 'Equitable access and value-based care' (9, 3.38); 'Contextually responsive care' (5, 3.35); 'Generating and moving evidence into practice' (11, 3.32); 'Health systems' (8, 3.28); 'Practice competence and sustainability' (5, 3.21); 'Education and professional development' (5, 3.17); and 'Professional identity' (8, 3.12). 'Research on the impact of rehabilitation on quality of life and reduction in care needs' was rated the most feasible statement, whereas 'Investigate strategies for physiotherapists to impact the political, social and economic environment of vulnerable and marginalised populations' was the least feasible statement. These findings are a resource for World Physiotherapy, the wider physiotherapy profession and key interest holder groups to inform research strategic direction, project development and advocacy.

titre: Functional Disability Among People with Schizophrenia in East Africa: A Systematic Review with Evidence Predominantly from Ethiopia.
titre_fr: Functional Disability Among People with Schizophrenia in East Africa: A Systematic Review with Evidence Predominantly from Ethiopia.
auteurs: Ndunguru Esterius Rabanus, Vivalya Bives Mutume Nzanzu, Posite Charles Malisaba, Usman Comfort Ojochenemi, Muhidin Hussen Abdu, Adeniyi Ismahil Adekunle, Eze Ejike Daniel, Usman Ibe Michael
resume: Schizophrenia causes substantial impairment in social, occupational, family, and everyday functioning. East African evidence is dispersed across disability scales, quality-of-life measures, employment outcomes, longitudinal studies, rehabilitation trials, and qualitative research. This review synthesized the magnitude, domains, correlates, measurement approaches, and rehabilitation evidence for functional disability among people with schizophrenia in East Africa. We conducted a PRISMA 2020 systematic review of studies involving people with schizophrenia in eight East African countries. Outcomes included disability, social and occupational functioning, activities of daily living, participation, functional recovery, and quality of life. We extracted study characteristics, outcomes, correlates, intervention findings, and qualitative themes, and assessed methodological quality using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. Fifteen publications from 2005 to 2025 were included; 14 (93.3%) were from Ethiopia and one (6.7%) from Rwanda, with no eligible publications identified from the other six prespecified East African countries. Cross-sectional studies predominated. Measures included WHOQOL-BREF, 36-item and 12-item WHODAS 2.0, SF-36, SOFAS, employment status, and qualitative approaches. Six publications had low risk-of-bias concern, eight had moderate concern, and one had high concern for causal or effect inference. Direct WHODAS evidence showed substantial disability, while longitudinal studies demonstrated persistent social and physical impairment. Negative symptoms, joblessness, prolonged untreated illness, substance use, weak social support, medication-related problems, and socioeconomic disadvantage were recurrent correlates. Community-based rehabilitation reduced disability in the cluster-randomized RISE trial. The available regional evidence is therefore heavily concentrated in Ethiopia. Functional impairment is multidimensional and extends beyond symptoms to work, social participation, daily activities, and quality of life. Integrated care should combine symptom management with rehabilitation, livelihood support, social inclusion, adherence support, and early treatment. Because the evidence is geographically concentrated in Ethiopia and uses heterogeneous measures, regional generalization should be cautious. Harmonized functional-outcome measurement and prospective multicountry research across East Africa are priorities.
resume_fr: Schizophrenia causes substantial impairment in social, occupational, family, and everyday functioning. East African evidence is dispersed across disability scales, quality-of-life measures, employment outcomes, longitudinal studies, rehabilitation trials, and qualitative research. This review synthesized the magnitude, domains, correlates, measurement approaches, and rehabilitation evidence for functional disability among people with schizophrenia in East Africa. We conducted a PRISMA 2020 systematic review of studies involving people with schizophrenia in eight East African countries. Outcomes included disability, social and occupational functioning, activities of daily living, participation, functional recovery, and quality of life. We extracted study characteristics, outcomes, correlates, intervention findings, and qualitative themes, and assessed methodological quality using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. Fifteen publications from 2005 to 2025 were included; 14 (93.3%) were from Ethiopia and one (6.7%) from Rwanda, with no eligible publications identified from the other six prespecified East African countries. Cross-sectional studies predominated. Measures included WHOQOL-BREF, 36-item and 12-item WHODAS 2.0, SF-36, SOFAS, employment status, and qualitative approaches. Six publications had low risk-of-bias concern, eight had moderate concern, and one had high concern for causal or effect inference. Direct WHODAS evidence showed substantial disability, while longitudinal studies demonstrated persistent social and physical impairment. Negative symptoms, joblessness, prolonged untreated illness, substance use, weak social support, medication-related problems, and socioeconomic disadvantage were recurrent correlates. Community-based rehabilitation reduced disability in the cluster-randomized RISE trial. The available regional evidence is therefore heavily concentrated in Ethiopia. Functional impairment is multidimensional and extends beyond symptoms to work, social participation, daily activities, and quality of life. Integrated care should combine symptom management with rehabilitation, livelihood support, social inclusion, adherence support, and early treatment. Because the evidence is geographically concentrated in Ethiopia and uses heterogeneous measures, regional generalization should be cautious. Harmonized functional-outcome measurement and prospective multicountry research across East Africa are priorities.

titre: Best Practices for Optimizing Recovery from Sepsis; Results of an Expert Panel.
titre_fr: Best Practices for Optimizing Recovery from Sepsis; Results of an Expert Panel.
auteurs: Sussman Jeremy B, Hogan Cainnear K, Whittington Taylor, Akgün Kathleen M, Anderson Mel L, Duseja Reena, Eaton Tammy L, Falvey Jason R, Ganz David A, McPeake Joanne, Taylor Stephanie Parks, Pawlikowski Scott, Piazza Kirstin M, Sullivan Sheila Cox, Bernstein Steven J, Prescott Hallie C
resume: Over one million patients survive sepsis annually in the USA. After sepsis, patients often experience new morbidity, with high rates of readmission and post-acute mortality. However, there are limited data to inform best practices to support recovery from sepsis. We convened an expert panel to rate the validity, importance, and resource intensity of 18 care practices aimed to support recovery from sepsis using the RAND/UCLA appropriateness method (a modified Delphi approach). The multidisciplinary panel consisted of 15 experts in sepsis, critical care, hospital medicine, primary care, geriatrics, nursing, and quality improvement, as well as Veteran patient representatives. In addition to the panel members' scores of care practices, panel deliberations were used to understand members' selections. Among the 18 care practices considered, all received agreement in final grading, 10 (56%) were rated as valid, and eight (44%) were rated as uncertain validity. Among 10 valid practices, five were rated as high importance and only moderately resource-intensive-suggesting they should be prioritized for implementation. The high-importance, moderate resource-intensity practices were as follows: scheduling recommended follow-up prior to discharge; screening for limitations in basic and instrumental activities of daily living (I/ADLs) and need for durable medical equipment (DME); educating patients on signs and symptoms of sepsis; educating patients on common symptoms after sepsis (e.g., fatigue, shortness of breath, brain fog); and counseling patients and/or caregivers on discharge medications and their indications. Study limitations include the panel composition (majority VHA clinicians, no social work representation), which may have impacted ratings. The expert panel used a validated method to prioritize care practices for supporting recovery from sepsis. These ratings can be used to improve management, inform quality improvement efforts, and guide resource allocation.

titre: H<sub>2</sub>FPEF Score and Charlson Comorbidity Index as Independent Predictors of Cardiovascular Outcomes in Elderly Patients Undergoing Geriatric Rehabilitation.
titre_fr: H<sub>2</sub>FPEF Score and Charlson Comorbidity Index as Independent Predictors of Cardiovascular Outcomes in Elderly Patients Undergoing Geriatric Rehabilitation.
auteurs: Dayer Nicolas, Auberson Denise, Lu Henri, Costa Elsa, Krief Hélène, Nguyen Sylvain, Major Kristof, Bosshard Wanda, Hullin Roger, Monney Pierre
resume: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is difficult to diagnose in older adults. The H<sub>2</sub>FPEF score estimates the likelihood of HFpEF and has been associated with adverse prognosis, but its performance has not been evaluated in geriatric inpatients with a high comorbidity burden. We hypothesized that the H<sub>2</sub>FPEF score predicts adverse outcomes in geriatric inpatients independently of comorbidity burden. This prospective cohort included consecutive patients admitted to a geriatric rehabilitation unit. All patients underwent functional and echocardiographic assessment at admission. The ability of the H<sub>2</sub>FPEF score, the Charlson comorbidity index (CCI), and their combination to predict 1-year all-cause mortality (ACM) or cardiovascular rehospitalization (CR) was evaluated. Among 302 patients (median age 83 years, 40% men), 24% had a H<sub>2</sub>FPEF score ≥ 6 indicating high HFpEF probability and 42% had a CCI > 3 indicating high comorbidity burden. The H<sub>2</sub>FPEF score correlated with CCI (β = 0.27, p < 0.01) and functional disability (lower Instrumental Activities of Daily Living score; β = -0.17, p = 0.003), but not with cognitive impairment. Both a high H<sub>2</sub>FPEF score and high CCI were associated with a higher risk of the combined outcome of 1-year ACM or CR (adjusted HR 2.89 [95% CI 1.63-5.10], p < 0.001 and adjusted HR 2.66 [95% CI 1.67-4.21], p < 0.001, respectively), with no interaction between them (p = 0.63). Patients with both high-risk scores had the highest risk (adjusted HR 4.66 [95% CI 2.54-8.57], p < 0.001). In geriatric inpatients, a high H<sub>2</sub>FPEF score is common and independently identifies patients at increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes at 1 year.

titre: Severity at the Gates: Or Why Prevention is the Aim of Reproductive Genetic Carrier Screening.
titre_fr: Severity at the Gates: Or Why Prevention is the Aim of Reproductive Genetic Carrier Screening.
auteurs: Ismaili M'hamdi Hafez
revue: The American journal of bioethics : AJOB
resume: Reproductive autonomy is usually described as the aim of publicly funded reproductive genetic carrier screening. I argue that this misdescribes the practice. These programs do not include conditions because any information might support choice. They include them because severity sets the scope. The aim of these programs, therefore, is prevention: not preventing the birth of particular persons, but offering a preventive response to the serious suffering associated with some severe inherited conditions. Reproductive autonomy, however, is the legitimate means by which a liberal program may pursue that aim, through information, counseling and voluntary decision making. That pursuit must satisfy what I call a liberal proviso, so that prevention does not become pressure, stigma or eugenic state steering. Naming prevention also enriches the disability critique. It makes both inclusion and exclusion morally visible and warranting justification, since both express judgments about which forms of suffering warrant collective response.

titre: Sarcopenia and Muscle Dysfunction in Older Adults with Burn Injuries: An Integrated Clinical Perspective.
titre_fr: Sarcopenia and Muscle Dysfunction in Older Adults with Burn Injuries: An Integrated Clinical Perspective.
auteurs: Santos-Costa Joana, Pinheiro João Páscoa, Cabral Luís, Santos-Faria João, Ribeiro Flávio, Caetano Marisa, Batista Juliana, Alexandrino Henrique, Branco João Paulo
resume: Sarcopenia is a progressive skeletal muscle disorder associated with impaired physical function and adverse outcomes in older adults. Burn injury imposes profound hypermetabolic and catabolic stress that may compromise muscle mass, strength, and physical function, particularly in individuals with reduced baseline muscle reserve. This narrative review integrates current evidence on sarcopenia and muscle dysfunction in older adults with burn injuries, addressing baseline vulnerability, burn-related muscle deterioration, diagnostic challenges, clinical implications, and therapeutic strategies. Patients may present with pre-existing sarcopenia or reduced muscle reserve, develop acute sarcopenia during or after burn-related illness, or experience worsening of pre-existing sarcopenia, potentially resulting in an acute-on-chronic trajectory. However, substantial burn-related muscle wasting, weakness, and functional impairment may occur without fulfilling diagnostic criteria for sarcopenia and represent distinct, clinically relevant manifestations of impaired muscle health. Sarcopenia assessment in burn patients is challenging and should be individualized according to clinical context and stage of recovery. Preservation and recovery of muscle health should be addressed throughout burn care through individualized nutritional support, early mobilization, and progressive exercise, with pharmacological strategies playing an adjunctive role. Prospective longitudinal studies are needed to characterize muscle-health trajectories, distinguish sarcopenia from other forms of post-burn muscle dysfunction, and determine their prognostic significance and response to interventions, including effects on functional recovery, independence, and quality of life.

titre: Locked in, Left Behind: Clinical, Psychosocial, and Ethical Dimensions of Prison Health-A Narrative Review.
titre_fr: Locked in, Left Behind: Clinical, Psychosocial, and Ethical Dimensions of Prison Health-A Narrative Review.
auteurs: Coman Adelina Ioana, Popa Marius Florentin, Deacu Sorin, Neculai-Candea Lavinia Simona, Gherase-Cristian Miruna, Radu Carmen Corina
resume: The global prison population has expanded over recent decades, straining correctional systems and positioning detention facilities as critical, yet frequently overlooked, sites of health inequity. With an estimated 11.5 million people currently incarcerated worldwide, prisons have become pivotal settings for examining the convergence of clinical vulnerability, psychosocial adversity, and human rights concerns. The aim of this narrative review was to examine how clinical, psychosocial, and bioethical factors interact to shape the health of incarcerated populations and to address four questions: (i) what is the burden and distribution of disease in correctional settings; (ii) which psychosocial consequences of confinement are most consistently reported and through which mechanisms; (iii) what bioethical tensions arise in the delivery of prison healthcare; and (iv) how do these patterns manifest across global, European, and Romanian contexts? We conducted an integrative narrative review reported against the SANRA criteria, searching PubMed, ScienceDirect and Scopus databases, alongside institutional sources from the World Health Organization, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the Council of Europe, and national correctional authorities, and synthesizing the evidence thematically across the three domains. The evidence indicates that incarcerated populations experience increased rates of infectious disease, chronic illness, mental disorders, and substance use disorders, combined with overcrowding, resource-limited healthcare systems, and restricted access to preventive care. Psychosocial stressors are consistently associated with elevated risk of anxiety, depression, self-harm, and suicide. Ethical tensions persist between institutional security requirements and the obligation to protect the autonomy, dignity, and right to healthcare of people deprived of liberty, equivalent to that available in the community. The contribution of this review is to integrate three literatures that are usually examined separately, the epidemiological, the psychosocial, and the bioethical, into a single conceptual framework spanning three nested levels of analysis and to apply that framework to a Central and Eastern European system that is under-represented in the prison health literature. Because the majority of incarcerated individuals eventually return to their communities, improving prison health is not solely a correctional priority but a public health and social justice imperative; the policy implications set out here follow from the broader literature synthesized in this review rather than from outcomes demonstrated by the review itself.

titre: Brain-computer interfaces: innovations and challenges in the field of cerebral palsy rehabilitation.
titre_fr: Brain-computer interfaces: innovations and challenges in the field of cerebral palsy rehabilitation.
auteurs: Chen Yize, Gao Yuling, Zhou Jiaqi, Zhang Zhenni, Zong Junwei, Liu Yong
resume: Brain-computer interfaces have shown great potential in the rehabilitation of Cerebral palsy, improving the ability of children with cerebral palsy to perform activities of daily living by replacing and restoring lost neurological functions, as well as accurately evaluating cognitive functions and facilitating rehabilitation in conjunction with various rehabilitation techniques. Nonetheless, numerous challenges persist in the application of brain-computer interfaces for cerebral palsy. Future research should focus on developing enhanced and more dependable brain-computer interfaces, advancing the hardware, and establishing ethical and regulatory frameworks to facilitate their utilisation in cerebral palsy rehabilitation.

titre: Artificial intelligence across the continuum of care for the aging musculoskeletal patient: From longitudinal phenotyping to personalized surgery and recovery monitoring.
titre_fr: Artificial intelligence across the continuum of care for the aging musculoskeletal patient: From longitudinal phenotyping to personalized surgery and recovery monitoring.
auteurs: Oettl Felix C, Zsidai Balint, Pruneski James A, Oeding Jacob F, Longo Umile Giuseppe, Hirschmann Michael T, Du Hyun Ro, Samuelsson Kristian
revue: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
resume: Musculoskeletal care is being reshaped by population aging, multimorbidity, frailty, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, polypharmacy and increasing vulnerability to postoperative loss of independence. Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered orthopaedic research, but its clinical translation remains constrained. Many models address isolated diagnostic, imaging or short-term prediction tasks rather than the longitudinal care trajectories that determine outcomes in older musculoskeletal patients. The central limitation is therefore not simply whether older adults are represented in datasets, but whether AI systems are valid across the continuum of geriatric orthopaedic care. This review argues for a transition from task-specific orthopaedic AI toward continuum-of-care AI for the aging musculoskeletal patient. Upstream, radiomics, longitudinal osteoarthritis phenotyping, opportunistic computed tomography (CT)-based skeletal assessment and AI-augmented dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) modelling may improve prediction of disease progression, fracture risk, treatment failure and surgical timing. At the point of intervention, AI-assisted arthroplasty planning may help move total knee arthroplasty from generic alignment targets toward phenotype-specific reconstruction strategies that account for constitutional alignment, bone morphology, ligament envelope, neuromuscular control, frailty and functional reserve. Perioperatively, automated frailty and sarcopenia phenotyping, wearable gait analysis and multimodal temporal models integrating imaging, electronic health records, laboratory data, medications, patient-reported outcomes and wearable signals may support dynamic risk prediction. After discharge, continuous monitoring of mobility, sleep, pain trajectories, wound-related symptoms and rehabilitation adherence may help close the high-risk surveillance gap during the 90-day postoperative episode. However, clinical adoption requires more than high discrimination. Explainable AI should be understood as one component of a broader trust framework that also includes calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision-curve analysis, external and prospective validation, workflow integration, post-deployment monitoring and accountability. The future of orthopaedic AI is not simply better diagnosis or more precise surgery, but longitudinal, multimodal support across the full care continuum: predicting progression, selecting treatment, personalizing surgery, optimizing perioperative care, monitoring recovery and preserving mobility and independence. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.

titre: Sensor-integrated AI-assisted gait training in dementia and Parkinson's disease: A single-session pre-post study.
titre_fr: Sensor-integrated AI-assisted gait training in dementia and Parkinson's disease: A single-session pre-post study.
auteurs: Hong Chien-Tai, Huang Li-Kai, Liu Cheng-Hsing, Chen Jia-Hung, Chan Lung
revue: Technology and health care : official journal of the European Society for Engineering and Medicine
resume: BackgroundGait impairment in dementia and Parkinson's disease (PD) contributes to falls, reduced mobility, and loss of independence. Sensor-integrated, AI-assisted gait training systems may provide standardized rehabilitation with real-time feedback and quantitative gait assessment.Objective: To investigate whether a single session of AI-assisted gait training improves spatiotemporal gait parameters in individuals with dementia and PD.MethodsThis single-session pre-post study enrolled ambulatory adults aged 60-85 years with dementia or PD. Participants completed one gait-training session using the Best Shape Gait (BSG) platform, with a planned duration of 15-30 min and the actual duration adjusted according to individual physical tolerance. Primary outcome was gait-speed change. Secondary outcomes included step length, step count, and gait variability. Paired t tests were performed within four predefined subgroups: Dementia-Support (n = 67), Dementia-Escort (n = 43), PD-Support (n = 64), and PD-Escort (n = 43).ResultsGait speed significantly increased after training across all predefined subgroups. In Support-mode walking, both dementia and PD cohorts demonstrated reduced step count and increased step length, suggesting improved locomotor efficiency. In Escort-mode walking, gait speed increased and step count decreased significantly in both cohorts, whereas changes in step length and gait variability were not significant. Gait variability did not significantly change in either cohort. Gait-speed improvement was consistent across dementia subtypes, modified Hoehn and Yahr stages, age groups, and fall-history categories. Baseline MMSE score and levodopa equivalent daily dose were not significantly associated with gait-speed improvement.ConclusionsA single session of sensor-integrated, AI-assisted gait training was associated with immediate within-session improvements in gait speed in individuals with dementia and PD. These findings support the feasibility of standardized, minimally supervised gait training in geriatric neurorehabilitation settings.
